articles.title: India’s EloElo nabs $80M from NBCUniversal to bet on the country’s rising microdrama market
articles.description: StoryTV has more than 33 million monthly active users according to Sensor Tower figures
articles.content: More than 118 million users watch microdramas every month as the serialized format has taken off in India. EloElo’s Story TV is one of the top apps for microdramas, with over 33 million active users, according to analysts. Banking on that scale, the company has raised $80 million in Series C from Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal. This round brings its total fundraising to $130 million, with a valuation of $500 million. As people spend more time on platforms hosting verticalized videos, serialized content has become popular in multiple geographies, including the U.S., China, and India, with Hollywood celebrities like Issa Rae, James Franco, and Kim Kardashian investing in and starring in the format. Given India’s massive internet population of more than a billion and the country’s appetite for entertainment content, it presents a big market opportunity, with analysts expecting the industry to cross $3-$4 billion in annual revenue by 2030. Last year, dedicated apps like Story TV, Kuku TV, and Quick TV were among the top downloaded video streaming apps in the country. Founded in 2020 by former Flipkart exec Saurabh Pandey, the Story TV platform has taken off in the last few years with a catalog of over 5,000 titles in six languages. Pandey told TechCrunch that because of the snackable content format, users log 95 minutes on the app on average through multiple sessions in a day. “I fundamentally believe that the next billion users will probably not grow up on a diet of watching television; they will grow up on a diet of watching content on their phones, right? And this content has to be, and this entertainment, designed very differently. It’s not going to be appointment viewing. It’s going to be within certain slots throughout the day. And a lot of this was earlier solved for short clips, but serialized storytelling was never solved,” Pandey said about the microdrama format. He believes that there still will be a place for big-screen viewing with family or friends, but the majority of entertainment consumption would be done through mobile. All microdrama platforms compete against platforms like YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok, where creators are posting content for free. Some of them are also creating a way for creators to post serialized content. Pandey thinks that producing quality content on the platform will entice users to choose StoryTV over other free platforms. The company points to its partnerships, such as the one with Indian TV production company Balaji Telefilms, to produce content. The company offers different kinds of subscriptions ranging from monthly, quarterly, and yearly to unlock content. It also offers some free content supported by ads, which might not be as lucrative a medium to make money as subscriptions, according to reports. Monetization is a challenge in India, as users often stick around for free content, but few convert to paid users. A report from analyst firm Redseer indicates that more than 40 million people have paid for microdrama at least once, but only 15-17 million users pay for it on a monthly basis. A separate survey by Ormax Media suggested that 72% of people haven’t ever paid while consuming microdrama. All microdrama platforms want to have enough supply to engage different audiences and want to involve AI to solve that. Some platforms, like Google-backed Kuku, want to improve workflows and create more content, and some platforms like Dashverse’s Shortfree want to use video AI models to create serialized clips. At the moment, StoryTV falls into the first camp with its Dolphin AI platform. Started as an internal tool to improve video creation, the company is now planning to make the tool widely available. It can act as an editor with templates and an array of models to create images, audio, and video, according to its website. EloElo’s vision is to have people use this tool for marketing campaigns and ads as well. Notably, while Indian platforms like Pocket and Kuku have built AI tools and given them to creators, it is likely to accelerate their content pipeline. But at InVideo, there hasn’t been a scaled effort to provide a good alternative to CapCut or Instagram Edits to creators from India. Pandey believes that human involvement is still paramount to producing good stories, and AI tools are still creative directors for steering. “My belief in involving AI is that AI is a really fast race car where AI is the engine, but you need an extremely capable Formula One driver to be on the steering wheel. That, for me, is the creative director or the showrunner. AI is supposed to work with them, augmenting their skill set. AI can help write stories, but so far the best stories I have loved have all had a very high human x AI element to it,” he said. Besides microdrama, the company also has a vertical video learning app, Master, competing with the likes of Seekho and Kuku’s Guru, and an AI companion app, Voxy AI. The company said that it has more than 40 million monthly users across its apps. While it didn’t bifurcate users by app, the majority of users belong to Story TV. EloElo currently has 240 people and wants to hire to increase the size of its AI and machine learning research team. The company is also deploying a good chunk of its capital to produce more original titles. MIT Investment Co., along with existing investors like Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures, and Griffin Gaming Partners, invested in the round. articles.title: In historic night, voters elect first Black woman, first Black Republican as governors
articles.description: Georgia voters elected the nation’s first Black woman governor on Tuesday while neighbors to the south in Florida became the first to elect a Black Republican governor. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first Democrat to occupy Georgia’s top office in more than two decades. In Florida, Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds […]
articles.content: Byron Donalds speaks at a rally in Tallahassee a week before Tuesday’s midterm election. Donalds made history becoming the nation’s first Black Republican elected to governor and the first Black candidate to win statewide office in Florida. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Georgia voters elected the nation’s first Black woman governor on Tuesday while neighbors to the south in Florida became the first to elect a Black Republican governor. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first Democrat to occupy Georgia’s top office in more than two decades. In Florida, Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds became the first Black person ever elected to statewide office there and the nation’s first elected Black Republican governor. Those historic victories were called early during Tuesday’s high-stakes midterm elections, when Democrats hoped to claw back state power from Republicans, who have controlled a majority of governorships and state legislatures for the last 16 years. A total of 36 gubernatorial elections were held Tuesday. As of 11:25 p.m. Eastern time, Democrats had won 14 of those contested races and Republicans had secured three, according to The Associated Press. For the first time ever, at least four Black governors will serve simultaneously in the United States, according to Tuesday’s unofficial results. Wisconsin voters also elected that state’s first Black governor, Democrat David Crowley. Lance Bottoms, Crowley and Donalds will join Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat, who easily won reelection Tuesday. The only Black Republican ever to serve as governor was Pinckney Benton Stewart Pinchback, who was appointed to lead Louisiana during Reconstruction beginning in 1872. The election also produced other firsts. Democrat Deb Haaland will become the nation’s first Native American woman to serve as governor after the former Interior Secretary won election in New Mexico. Haaland is an enrolled member of the Pueblo of Laguna. New Mexico will be the second state led by a Native American governor following Oklahoma, where current Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt is an enrolled member of the Cherokee Nation and former Gov. Johnston Murray was a member of the Chickasaw Nation. Dr. Amy Acton became the first woman elected governor of Ohio — and the first Democrat to lead the state in 20 years. And in Texas, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa will become the nation’s third Latina governor and the first to lead her state. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott conceded at 11 p.m. Eastern Tuesday, according to the Texas Tribune. Only two other Hispanic women have ever served as governor, both in New Mexico: Current Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and former Republican Gov. Susana Martinez. Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org. articles.content: Michigan state Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit) speaks at a rally advocating against a proposed 24% wholesale tax on marijuana for the next fiscal year. Sept. 30, 2025 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceState Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit) will succeed U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar to represent Michigan’s 13th Congressional District. McKinney defeated Republican T.P. Nykoriak with 75.5% of the vote, according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press, which called the race at 10:33 p.m.. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel congratulated McKinney on his victory in a statement. “As a labor organizer and state representative, Donavan has the values and experience we need to fight and deliver for Detroiters in the halls of Congress. His leadership will be key to making the wealthy pay their fair share, expanding access to healthcare and housing, and making sure every Michigander has a fair shot, no matter their zip code.” The Working Families Party, a minor political party backing progressive candidates, also cheered McKinney’s victory. “WFP champion Donavan McKinney defeated a sitting Congressman in the primary, despite millions in spending from corporate and crypto interests,” Branden Snyder, state director for the Michigan Working Families Party, said in a statement. “ Now he’s heading to Congress to fight for the community that raised him. We know that Donavan will fight with everything he has to protect the rights of workers and unions, stand up to corporate greed, and bring back investments to Michigan’s 13th Congressional District.” This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

articles.title: Detroiters with disabilities successfully cast ballots after primary woes
articles.description: Detroiters with blindness, low-vision and physical disabilities have raised the alarm about unreliable voting machines and polling place access in recent weeks. Here's what happened on Election Day.
articles.content: Detroit Free Press is a partner and shares a reporter with BridgeDetroit. Stories shared are not under a paywall. Detroit Free Press Sabrina Rice was in tears after she fed her ballot into the tabulator on Tuesday afternoon. She was finally able to vote by herself and was excited. Rice, who has been blind for about 15 years, hasn’t voted on her own for a long time because machines designed to allow voters to cast ballots independently had malfunctioned. “It’s been a number of years since I’ve voted secretly and independently,” said Rice, of Detroit, after casting her ballot at the Unity Baptist Church. Because she’d voted while she had her sight, she didn’t think there should be a change because she lost it. Later that day, over at another polling location, Edison Elementary School, Richard Clay was just as pleased. “This was a very good voting experience,” said Clay, president of the Detroit Advocates of the Blind. Detroiter Richard Clay voted using a VAT at Edison Elementary School on Election Day. Clay is the president of Detroit Advocates of the Blind. (Credit: Johnathan Shephard for BridgeDetroit) During the August primary, what’s known as the voter assist terminal (VAT) — a device with accommodations designed to allow people to vote independently and secretly — failed, even after several attempts that took about an hour, he said. A poll worker had to help Clay fill out his ballot. It’s an experience that left him feeling angry, disappointed and stripped of his rights as a voter. Rice and her husband, Darryl Rice, who is also blind, waited three and a half hours during the primary and didn’t end up voting because the machine didn’t work. Sabrina and Darryl Rice, a husband-and-wife pair who are both blind, voted using a VAT at Unity Baptist Church on Election Day. (Credit: Johnathan Shephard for BridgeDetroit) They were among the Detroiters who raised the alarm about accessibility at the polls in recent weeks. In late September, members of the blind community told Detroit City Council about their experiences with unreliable voting devices, saying the machines froze or they experienced long delays, and sought a change ahead of the November election. The Free Press and BridgeDetroit followed several voters on Election Day as they cast their ballots using VATs. “It feels very, very good to see that the hard work that we’ve been putting in has paid off and that this VAT machine, which was not working just a couple of months ago (is) now working today,” said Clay. He estimates that, over the past 5 years, the VAT has worked 40% of the time at his polling place. Clay, who has been blind since the age of 2, makes a concerted effort to vote in person to monitor how accessible the polls are for those who are blind. People with disabilities are “full-fledged members of our community.” Detroiters who successfully used VATs on Tuesday left their polling locations relieved and excited but wondered what future elections would hold and what was happening at other precincts. “When it’s time to vote again, will the machine work? That’s the only thing going through my head. We made it through this time, but what’s going to happen next time, because every time it’s a different process,” said Darryl Rice. A 2025 audit of 415 polling locations across 7 counties by Detroit Disability Power found that 10% met accessibility standards. Thirty-six percent were found to have fully functional VATs, down from 62% the year before. “Many of the sites that are inaccessible need capital improvements to get a ramp or get an elevator or have automatic doors or get a repaved parking lot — those are all things that are expensive, and that really could require state legislative action to address,” said Dessa Cosma, executive director of Detroit Disability Power. But many issues are “no cost, game decisions” that are easily solvable, including not using a barrel to prop a door open, having better signage, ensuring the wheelchair height voting booth is set up and that the VAT is turned on and the person in charge of it knows how to use it, Cosma said. Polling places and early voting sites are required to have a VAT, which includes such features as audio ballots for those who are blind and large print displays. The Detroit Department of Elections told BridgeDetroit in late September that there are VATs at all of the city’s 158 polling locations and additional machines in reserve. The department said complaints about VATS are not made often, but when they are, a team is dispatched. The elections office said a specialist trained on how to operate the VATs by the elections department staff is stationed at each polling spot. Marguerite Maddox voted with the assistance of Kaci Pellar, her trusted friend at the Walker Williams Rec Center on Election Day (Credit: Bryce Huffman, BridgeDetroit) Detroiter Marguerite Maddox said she was “very anxious” because she wasn’t sure how many voters would come out to the polls. She’d been stuck in line for a while, but once she got to the VAT, the process was smooth, she said. “Between A ,B and C, I’d give the VAT machines a B today,” said Maddox, who uses a walker and has a service dog. Maddox voted with the assistance of Kaci Pellar, her trusted friend at the Walker Williams Rec Center. Maddox, who has cerebral palsy, is a regular fixture at council meetings and a disability justice advocate. It took between 30 to 40 minutes to fill out her ballot, she said, whereas in some previous elections it would take her up to 3 hours. She’d like to see more precinct tables at polling places to make the lines shorter for everyone. On Tuesday, Stephen Handschu was also able to successfully cast his ballot using a VAT at Central United Methodist Church. “We are no different than the rest of the population in valuing that kind of repeated neighborhood personal human contact,” Handschu previously told BridgeDetroit. “There’s something very powerful, I think, about making it to the polling place with other voters. It’s one of the few times that you’re putting your little hand on a very big oar and trying to pull it in a certain direction.” Stephen Handschu, an artist and representative of Detroit Advocated of the Blind, voted using a VAT at Central United Methodist Church on Election Day. (Credit: Bryce Huffman, BridgeDetroit) Handschu, an artist and representative for Detroit Advocates of the Blind, had stopped voting in person because the VAT didn’t work. One year, there were no headphones. There were times when the machines just didn’t turn on, he said. He begrudgingly voted absentee. He intended to vote in person, partly because he wanted to see if the system would work as it should and partly because he wanted to cast his ballot alongside his neighbors. The ballot was long and using the machine was cumbersome, he said. The process took him nearly two hours, but he was happy the machine worked this time. “No one should take for granted the right to vote to begin with, and the right to vote secretly,” said Handschu. “Those are pretty important rights of citizenship. And what can I say? I wish we didn’t have to fuss so long to get here, but I’m delighted we got here. And at least today for me, the system did work.” BridgeDetroit’s Bryce Huffman and Christine Ferretti contributed to this report.

articles.title: NYC Voters Pass Ballot Measures That Could Boost Zohran Mamdani’s Agenda
articles.content: The five proposals on New York City voters’ ballots are the result of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s Commission on Government Efficiency. LEONARDO MUNOZ/AFP via Getty Images New York City voters gave a confident “yes” to all five of the ballot measures put forward by Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s first Charter Revision Commission, approving the slate of proposals intended to streamline government processes and help the city better plan for its financial future. The New York Times reported all five proposals passed shortly before 11 p.m., but signs were strong earlier in the night too. With more than 88% of scanners reporting nearly an hour after polls closed, the first four proposals, which would cut some of the red tape associated with creating bike lanes, expanding outdoor dining, starting construction projects and hiring city contractors, held between 61% and 67% of the vote, according to unofficial results from the city Board of Elections. The fifth proposal, which would set contribution goals for the city’s rainy day fund, held at roughly 72% of the vote. The proposals were crafted by a 15-member panel Mamdani assembled last spring, which he dubbed the Commission on Government Efficiency, or COGE – a cheeky play on President Donald Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency. The group held a series of public meetings across the city, seeking feedback from residents on how they might amend the City Charter to make city government more effective. Voters’ approval of the proposals doesn’t exactly come as a surprise. Historically, most ballot proposals pass – even ones more controversial than these five, like the housing related proposals on last year’s ballot. While the City Council waged war with the Adams administration over those questions aimed at reshaping the land use process, the legislative body refrained from taking a collective position this time around. That doesn’t mean they garnered universal acclaim. Republicans were generally opposed, as was the New York Post’s Editorial Board. Some civic groups took issue with the rainy day fund proposal, arguing it didn’t go far enough to strengthen the city’s reserves. For the most part though, civic groups and Mamdani’s allies trumpeted all five of the proposals as measured, practical steps that would streamline city government. The proposals amount to another victory for the 35-year-old democratic socialist mayor. Mamdani’s creation of the commission effectively slammed the door on the zombie-like charter revision commission formed by former Mayor Eric Adams on his final day in office. With the help of former first deputy mayor Randy Mastro, the group sought to put questions on the ballot that could make things harder for Mamdani. The mayor has danced around outwardly promoting the proposals, and appears to be heeding the city’s rules barring the use of governmental funds or resources to produce marketing material encouraging voters to vote a certain way. The social media ads and informational resources put out by the Mamdani administration describe the proposals, albeit with positive language, without telling New Yorkers to vote one way or another. Still, some good government groups want tighter guidance around electioneering. “People are walking right up to the line and not crossing it in terms of saying ‘vote yes, vote no,’ and we’ve seen that repeatedly,” said Rachael Fauss, senior policy adviser at Reinvent Albany. “(Mamdani’s ads are) clearly aimed to influence a voter to make a certain choice, and we think there needs to be better enforcement and rules on this.” The Mamdani administration did not see their ad campaign for the ballot proposals as electioneering, but rather their duty as charged to them in the state Municipal Home Rule law. “Per state law, the Commission is charged with providing public education and is leveraging the tools available to inform New Yorkers about the proposed ballot props in an effort to encourage them to make their voices heard," City Hall spokesperson Dora Pekec said in a statement. This story has been updated to reflect that the results on all five ballot proposals have been called. NEXT STORY: Hochul cruises to reelection

Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield) emerged victorious against Troy Mayor Ethan Baker, receiving 59.6% of the vote, according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press at 9:33 p.m. Moss, the state’s first openly gay state senator, will be Michigan’s first openly LGBTQ+ representative in Congress. Jeremy will take his resilience and legislative experience to continue serving Michiganders in the halls of Congress by lowering costs, protecting our freedoms, and holding the Trump administration accountable.” This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available. 11:32 pmThis story has been updated with comment from Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel Jr.

articles.title: Mamdani endorsed congressional candidates win House elections
articles.content: NEW YORK (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani endorsed three progressives for Congress in the June primary and all three have won their blue districts on Election Day, ABC News projects. They include Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Brad Lander, and two of the candidates successfully backed by Mamdani are democratic socialists. State Assembly Member Claire Valdez, who was running to represent New York's 7th Congressional District, was projected to beat out Republican Melvin Rivera and Priscilla Ghaznavi. In the primary for retiring U.S. Rep. Nydia Velázquez's seat, Valdez beat out Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso. In the race for New York's 13th Congressional District, Chevalier, another Mamdani-backed democratic socialist, was projected to defeat Republican Jomo M. Williams. Back in June, Democratic U.S. Rep. Adriano Espaillat lost his bid for reelection to Chevalier. She hasn't held public office before and once helped organize pro-Palestinian protests at Columbia University. A third candidate backed by Mamdani, former city comptroller Brad Lander, was projected to defeat Republican Jennifer Moore in New York's 10th Congressional District.

articles.title: 2026 elections: Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed projected to win Michigan Senate race
articles.content: BERRIEN COUNTY, Mich. -- In the early hours of Wednesday morning, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed addressed supporters and claimed victory over Republican Mike Rogers, in his bid to become the first-ever Muslim senator. "They went all in on one of the ugliest campaigns we've seen in our lifetimes," he said of Republicans. "They might have been pointing to my name and my faith, but we all know that my name and my faith aren't the reason you can't afford your gas, not the reason you can't afford your groceries, not the reason you can't see a doctor." "Now, as I was campaigning, some of you would come up and ask, 'How come you don't hit back? How come you don't call them racist or hateful?' Because here's the thing: I didn't run for myself, and in truth, they weren't targeting me," he said. "They weren't just attacking me. They were targeting and attacking you. They were targeting and attacking the very idea of America." "They hate the idea of an America big enough for anyone who looks a little different, or prays a little different, or whose family comes from a different part of the world. That includes me, but it also includes anyone and everyone who doesn't look like them, pray like them, love like them, or isn't rich like them," he continued. El-Sayed directly addressed some of his prominent critics. To his opponent Rogers, he said, "So, Mike, enjoy your retirement. I know you got a house in Florida and two yachts. See, you chose hate, and Michigan chose hope. May we never have to see the likes of you in the state again." He also addressed Vice President VD Vance, using a term of endearment and saying, "JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January. So you know what that means, Wolverine one, Buckeye zero." To President Donald Trump, El-Sayed said, "Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name, so after JD swears me in in January, you could just go on and call me senator." El-Sayed also addressed allegations that his critical stance on Israel is antisemitic. "They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars. If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination that's not hate, it's love," he said.

articles.title: Michigan elections: Voters approve Proposal 2 Money Out of Politics question
articles.description: Voters on Tuesday were asked to consider a ballot proposal that would prohibit regulated utilities and large state contractors from contributing to Michigan politicians.
articles.content: Michigan’s Proposal 2 passed, limiting corporate spending in Michigan politics Supporters say the measure will remove the influence of deep-pocketed special interests, while detractors say it will stifle free speech Opponents swiftly sued to try to stop some aspects of the measure The ballot measure to limit corporate spending in Michigan’s political arena passed by an overwhelming margin on Tuesday and was immediately met with a lawsuit from opponents. The Associated Press declared the proposal passed at about 9:45 p.m., with 4 out of every 5 votes supporting the measure in early returns. By 10:10 p.m., the conservative nonprofit Mackinac Center for Public Policy had filed a lawsuit contending the measure is unconstitutional and seeking to block parts of it from being implemented. Backers of Proposal 2, sponsored by the group Michiganders for Money Out of Politics, called its resounding victory a “mandate for change” that Michigan lawmakers should heed. “Our representatives failed to deliver on holding corrupt pay-to-play politics accountable, so we said enough,” said Christy McGillivray, executive director of the group Voters Not Politicians. “And tonight, Michiganders delivered.” Officials with the Mackinac Center called the measure “a nasty tool” that can be used to punish people for “daring to speak their minds.” The lawsuit, which names Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Attorney General Dana Nessel as defendants, was filed in the US District Court for the Western District of Michigan. The new law will prohibit monopoly electric utilities, companies with more than $250,000 in state government contracts and people with close connections to those companies from directly or indirectly contributing to Michigan politicians. Supporters of the measure, including voter advocacy, environmental and racial justice groups, argued it offers a needed check on corporate lobbyists’ influence in Lansing. RELATED: Donate Initiative aims to reveal ‘dark money’ donors behind political ads Fact check: Would ‘money out of politics’ proposal stifle free speech? Fact check: Would ‘money out of politics’ proposal live up to its name? That message resonated with voters like 26-year-old Emily Rose of Mason. Michigan’s monopoly utilities “make a lot of money off of us,” Rose said. “And if they’re using that money to support politics, that doesn’t really do us any favors as the people paying those bills.” Opponents, including business groups and utilities, argued it violates corporations’ right to free speech and gives unions and out-of-state donors an unfair advantage. They point to past court cases, including the US Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United ruling that gave corporations the right to make unlimited political expenditures. Officials for Michiganders for Money Out of Politics say they carefully worded the measure to withstand legal challenges. For instance, it doesn’t address contributions to super PACs that are allowed under Citizens United, and it specifies that if courts void any portion of the proposal, “the remaining portions remain in effect.” Here’s what to know: What’s in the measure Proposal 2 expands upon Michigan’s existing prohibition on direct corporate contributions to Michigan candidates while also including company officials, board members and people with “substantial” ownership interests in the companies targeted by the ballot measure. They’re barred from funding candidates for governor, attorney general or the state Legislature, members of the Michigan Public Service Commission, state or local political party committees and certain committees that contribute to candidates. The new law also eliminates some avenues through which corporations pay for politicians’ travel and meals. What’s left out Proposal 2 does not stop dark money spending by corporations through 501(c)(4) nonprofit organizations, which generally do not have to disclose their donors. However, it does require dark money groups to report donors if they run advertisements referencing a candidate or ballot issue within 100 days of a general election or 30 days before a primary. What they’re saying Proponents have described the initiative as a first step toward tamping down on corporate influence in politics, while contending further action is needed. “There will need to be more reforms after we pass this ballot initiative,” Proposal 2 organizer Sean McBrearty previously told Bridge Michigan. “But this ballot initiative, we designed to take out the biggest chunk that we can.” But opponents contend the law’s incomplete reach would put Michigan corporations at a disadvantage in the quest to influence policy, because money could still flow from unions and out-of-state donors who aren’t state contractors. “This egregious proposal appears to silence the voices of job providers and limit free speech for some while giving others, like labor unions, a free pass,” the Michigan Chamber of Commerce previously said. The Mackinac Center’s lawsuit challenges two aspects of the law: its requirement for groups to disclose donors if they reference a candidate or ballot issue close to an election and a provision that could trigger campaign finance requirements for organizations publishing content that promotes, supports, attacks or opposes a candidate or ballot question. The group contends those provisions could inappropriately force a wide variety of organizations and media outlets to disclose their donors. “Michiganders shouldn’t face fines or jail just so that they can discuss politicians, policy, or elections,” said Patrick J. Wright, vice president of the Mackinac Center Legal Foundation. “These rules threaten access to information voters rely on and violate the privacy of people who support organizations they believe in.” Click here to read the full text of Proposal 2

articles.content: Michigan will restrict political contributions by the state's utilities and big government contractors. articles.title: Michigan Proposal 1 fails as voters say ‘no’ to constitutional convention
articles.description: Michiganders reject proposal to begin the process of rewriting Michigan’s 63-year-old constitution.
articles.content: Michigan Proposal 1 failed. Measure proposed a new convention to rewrite Michigan’s 63-year-old constitution A diverse coalition spent $3 million opposing the measure Voters have repeatedly rejected proposals to rewrite the constitution Michiganders adopted in 1963 Michigan voters on Tuesday resoundingly rejected a ballot proposal that would have led to a rewrite of the state Constitution. The Associated Press declared the proposal failed at about 9:45 p.m., with 3 out of every 4 votes opposing the measure in early returns. The proposal asking voters to convene a constitutional convention automatically appears on Michiganders’ ballots every 16 years and has not succeeded in more than six decades. Michigan’s current constitution was adopted in 1963. Voter Jerrilyn Mathews of Manton was among voters who opposed the proposal. “You open everything up, and whoever’s in power now gets to change everything,” Mathews told Bridge, explaining her opposition. “That’s not the way it should be.” A diverse coalition including labor, business and issue advocacy groups spent nearly $3 million urging voters to oppose the measure, contending the lengthy process to revise Michigan’s constitution would waste money and give special interests a chance to radically alter the document. They raised fears that reopening the document could lead to the overturning of voter-approved provisions, such as the 2022 amendment that enshrined abortion access. The opposition group, a coalition of special interest groups ironically calling itself Protect MI Constitution from Special Interests, celebrated Tuesday’s outcome as a victory for taxpayers and democracy. “Today’s vote reflects a shared belief that Michigan’s energy is best spent solving problems, not creating new uncertainty,” said Wendy Block, executive vice president of business advocacy for the Michigan Chamber of Commerce. “We were proud to stand alongside business, labor, education, and community partners in support of that vision.”Donate RELATED: Proposal 1: Rewrite Michigan’s Constitution? Here’s how it would work Michigan Proposal 1 and 2: What to know about statewide ballot measures Fact check: Would ‘money out of politics’ proposal stifle free speech? There was little organized support for the proposal, although some influential Michiganders such as Republican state Sen. Ed McBroom urged a “yes” vote. They argued a convention could force conversations about issues that may have bipartisan voter support but get limited attention in Lansing. Among them: data centers and dark money in politics. “There’s this unholy alliance of Lansing swamp creatures who are opposed to (a convention) — but normal Michiganders seem to support it,” Republican political consultant Dennis Lennox told Bridge Michigan in September. Proposal 1 would have triggered a lengthy process: First, Michigan’s political parties would have held primaries to nominate convention delegates. Next, Michigan would have held a general election by mid-2027 to select a delegate for each of Michigan’s 148 House and Senate districts. The Legislature would have needed to decide how much convention delegates were paid. Then, delegates would have then convened in Lansing by Oct. 5, 2027, triggering a constitutional review process with no set end date. They would have appointed officers, hired staff, debated what to add or remove from Michigan’s constitution and eventually proposed a rewrite for voters to consider. Within 90 days after the convention adjourned, Michigan voters would have weighed another ballot proposal asking whether they wanted to adopt the convention’s proposed new constitution. The nonpartisan state Senate Fiscal Agency estimated it would have cost Michigan $80 million to hold a convention. The last time voters considered the constitutional convention proposal, in 2010, 33% of voters supported the idea. However, voters have repeatedly amended the constitution through ballot initiatives. Click here to read the full text of Proposal 1

articles.content: Michiganders for Money Out of Politics submitted its signatures in Lansing to make the November 2026 ballot. May 27, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Proposal 2 on Michigan ballots, the “Michiganders for Money Out of Politics” initiative, has passed. The initiative will alter state campaign finance law to ban campaign spending from “regulated electric and gas utilities, contractors with over $250,000 annually in government contracts, and people and organizations with substantial connections to those utilities or contractors.” Meanwhile, Proposal 1, a ballot measure asking Michigan voters if they want to call a constitutional convention, has failed, with the measure having garnered significant opposition from a wide range of groups. Proposal 2 succeeded by a 62-point margin, with unofficial results showing “yes” votes taking 81.2% of the vote as of 9:38 p.m., when the race was called by the Associated Press, with less than 10% of the vote in. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE “Tonight, David beat Goliath,” said Ken Whittaker of Michigan United, when Michiganders for Money Out of Politics claimed victory just after 9 p.m. Christy McGillivray, executive director of Voters Not Politicians and a co-chair of the ballot effort, said the results show that there are limits to corporate power. “We’re the ones that make change. Our representatives failed to deliver on holding corrupt pay to play politics accountable, so we said enough. And tonight Michiganders delivered,” McGillivray. The ballot proposal had broad support in polling leading up to Election Day and throughout the election cycle. Republican leadership in the state House had sought to keep the measure off the ballot by passing a version of it into statute in the Legislature, a move that Democrats said could have made it easier to amend or overturn later. However, Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks — also the Democratic lieutenant governor nominee — declined to take it up in the Senate, leaving the decision to the voters. An opposition group to the measure, Protect MI Free Speech, had filed a lawsuit against the Board of State Canvassers alleging that the ballot petition did not meet the threshold of valid signatures required to put it on the ballot. The Michigan Supreme Court declined to hear the lawsuit in early September. The constitutional convention proposal failed by a 50-point margin, with unofficial results showing “no” votes taking 75.5% of the vote as of 9:40 p.m., when the race was called by the Associated Press, with 15% of votes counted. The measure is constitutionally mandated to appear on the ballot every 16 years, but has not passed since 1961, when Michigan’s current state constitution was crafted. The last three times the question was on the ballot — 1978, 1994 and 2010 — the measure failed by wide margins, similar to Tuesday’s early returns. The measure faced an ideologically broad opposition movement, with groups ranging from Planned Parenthood of Michigan to Right to Life of Michigan coming out in opposition. Much of the opposition to the prospect of a convention came from concerns that it would have allowed special interest groups to exert their influence over the convention process and put in place new constitutional measures that would be beneficial to them. Following news that it had been defeated, the group organizing the opposition, Protect MI Constitution from Special Interests, issued a simple statement: “THANK YOU! WE DID IT — TOGETHER.” “We’ve never seen this many business groups, labor unions, educators and advocates, who disagree on plenty of issues working, side by side on the same campaign. These organizations recognized a common cause, brought their own networks and perspectives to the table, and worked together toward this important goal. That kind of partnership doesn’t happen every day, and these results show what it can accomplish,” John Sellek, CEO and chief strategist of Harbor Strategic, said.

articles.title: The Scenes From East Lansing’s Midterm Election
articles.description: View ELi's gallery from around town during Tuesday's midterm election.
articles.content: Election Day is here. For those who have not voted early, today is the last day to submit a ballot. Across the state, hundreds of poll workers are stationed at voting locations. At the same time, poll watchers, challengers, and members of the public are engaging with the election process. Outside of the Hannah Community Center, individuals from different organizations sat at least 100-feet from the entrance, including volunteers with Rep. Tom Barrett’s campaign. “We’re just out here talking to undecided voters and seeing if people have any questions about [Barrett],” one volunteer, who declined to be identified, told City Pulse. “It’s mostly just them trying to get an understanding of where [Barrett’s] priorities lie, so they don’t have specific policy questions,” he said. According to the volunteer, “plenty of people” had stopped at the table throughout the morning. Inside the polling site, Lindsay Oswald, a precinct co-chair, said the day was running smoothly. “[Voters] have been asking normal voter questions about where they should go next and how to fill out the ballot,” she said. Oswald said there were a couple of poll watchers at the site, but was unsure about U.S. Department of Justice monitors. In October, the department sent notices to seven Michigan municipalities, including Lansing and East Lansing, informing them that DOJ monitors would be present at certain polling locations. Monitors are considered poll watchers and cannot speak with constituents inside of the voting site, touch election equipment or ballots, or interfere with election administration. At the Gier Community Center, precinct chairperson Jill Dombrowski said DOJ monitors and Secretary of State officials were at the center earlier in the day. “They were following procedure. They were respectful.” She noted that the DOJ monitors conducted exit polling once they left the center. “Which is allowed,” she said, “but it is something we want to kind of keep an eye on.” “Since the [DOJ] people were here, then the [state officials] people were here to watch to make sure they were doing okay.” Dombrowski has worked elections since 2016. Constituents are more attuned to the details of the election process this midterm season, she said. “We have these signs printed that say ‘No campaigning within 100 feet of the voter entrance,’ and someone actually called the Secretary of State to say this sign … wasn’t far enough away.” “We put our 100-foot sign at the 100-foot mark,” Dombrowski said, pointing to a sign closer to the center’s parking lot. “We just put this here because maybe they weren’t able to see that one [over there].” According to Dombrowski, that level of attention to detail is out of the norm. “But each election is its own special snowflake,” she said. Throughout the morning, the center had a handful of poll watchers from nonpartisan groups, and one challenger from the Michigan Republican Party. And even with other voting options available, Dombrowski said it’s great to see the community participate in the election process. “It’s just wonderful to see so many people want to come in person … all the election workers, that’s why we’re here.” Polls close at 8 p.m., but voting continues until the last person in line has submitted their ballot.

articles.title: ELECTION DAY 2026: Turnout expected at 40-45%, no DOJ interference at polls, official says
articles.description: Check back for results as they come in.
articles.content: LIVE RESULTS: Detroit | Wayne County Voter turnout in Detroit is expected to fall between 40-45% once every ballot is counted and there were no issues with government interference at the polls, according to Department of Elections Chief Daniel Baxter. Baxter spoke during a press conference from the Central Counting Board at Huntington Place Tuesday shortly after 8:30 p.m., outlining the tabulation process and what observers are going to see. He said the anticipated turnout is on par with what Detroit would typically see for midterm gubernatorial race. So far, the voting totals are as follows: 25,500 Detroiters voted early at in-person locations between Oct. 24 and Nov. 2. 110,000 Detroiters who voted on Election Day at 502 precincts across the city. 68,000 Detroiters submitted absentee ballots The city expects to post its first results by 9:30 p.m., with a goal of having 90-95% of results reported by 11 p.m., Baxter said. As he was speaking, Baxter said he expected the largest shipment of the night of ballots, with 1,300, on what he described as “the big truck” to be in at any time. The final delivery will come in later. As for concerns that poll watchers from the Department of Justice could interfere with elections, Baxter said “absolutely not.” “There were 13 teams, 2 people per team, 26 folks, and then we had representatives from the US Congress who were here to observe the operation, as well. Is that unique, absolutely not,” he said. “In the 2024 election, we had some people here from Congress. In 2024, we had the representatives from the Department of Justice. We did not have as many back in 2024 or in previous elections.” Baxter added: Every voter in the city of Detroit had an opportunity to cast their ballot without being impacted by their presence. Poll workers tally votes at Huntington Place on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Jena Brooker, BridgeDetroit 8 p.m. Polls have now closed in Detroit. The attention now shifts to Huntington Place, where the vote count will take place. BridgeDetroit is on the scene and will bring you updates. For now, stay with us for results as they come in: Michigan US Senate election results: Abdul El-Sayed vs Mike Rogers Detroit voters to elect new school board majority in consequential election Michigan governor’s race election results: Jocelyn Benson vs. John James Michigan secretary of state race: Garlin Gilchrist faces Anthony Forlini Michigan election results: Governor, Senate, US House, proposals, more Michigan attorney general election: Doug Lloyd faces Eli Savit Michigan elections: Voters decide makeup of Michigan Supreme Court Michigan elections: Voters make picks for State Board of Eduction, university boards Michigan elections: Voters decide on Proposal 2 Money Out of Politics question Michigan elections: Voters decide Proposal 1 constitutional convention measure Voters at St. Suzanne Cody Rouge Community Resource Center on Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Micah Walker for BridgeDetroit 3:45 p.m. — Tuesday, Nov. 3 Detroit voters on Tuesday will decide a new majority for the city’s public school board, in races that will shape the district’s future. While many at the polls said that they want to see strong board representation for the city’s schoolchildren, most said they were unsure who to vote for. Katherine Jackson, a 72-year-old retiree, cast her vote at Detroit Lions Academy on the city’s west side Tuesday afternoon. She said she was eager to support Democrats. But when it came to the races for the Detroit Public Schools Community District – which her grandchildren attend – she said she’s not as informed on the board candidates as she hoped she could have been. “I really wish there was someone or something to help me so I just voted for the names I recognized,” she told BridgeDetroit. Detroiters will vote to fill five open at-large seats on the DPSCD’s seven-member board, including four seats with full four-year terms and one with a two-year partial term. Adrian Christianson, 21, a young voter in the city’s Warrendale neighborhood, turned up to cast his ballot at Carver STEM Academy Tuesday, citing concerns over the economy and federal immigration enforcement. The Wayne State University student said the school board race was also important to him. As an education major, he believes students deserve a quality education and that teachers deserve more support. “As trivial as some people might see it, I think it’s very big because the kids are the future,” said Christianson, who did not disclose his selections for the board. Voters line up to cast ballots at Carver Stem Academy on Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Micah Walker, BridgeDetroit BridgeDetroit asked several other voters at the polls Tuesday what they thought about the DPSCD school board race. Many said they were not familiar and had little knowledge of the candidates. Terrence Barker, who voted at St. Suzanne Cody Rouge Community Resource Center, said he also wasn’t familiar with the candidates for the DPSCD school board but more funding needs to go to the district, citing things like schools not having air conditioning. “Where is the money going?” He said. “It’s definitely not hitting the inner city.” Elizabeth Gist, 40, voted at Detroit Unity Temple near Palmer Park. Gist said she believes in voting but is ambivalent about its impact at the same time, given promises that end up broken by candidates once they reach office. It’s hard to know who can be trusted, even harder in the age of AI, she said when “I don’t know who wrote these responses,” on campaign websites. Gist said above the statewide and national races on the ballot, she cared most about local issues, including electing DPSCD board members. She said she spent a lot of time researching since she hadn’t heard much from any campaign, and selected about seven school board candidates she planned to vote for. She hopes they can improve Detroit’s educational system and its children’s outcomes. “Children are the future…and I’m concerned. Because critical thinking seems to be a lost art. Even basic phonics, reading, arithmetic,” Gist said. Blind Detroit voter casts ballot independently amid accessibility concerns 2:15 p.m. — Tuesday, Nov. 3 Stephen Handschu shared frustrations ahead of the midterm election about unreliable equipment that often kept Detroiters with disabilities from voting independently at the polls. On Tuesday, the 79-year-old blind Detroiter was able to successfully cast his ballot on a Voter Assist Terminal (VAT) at Central United Methodist Church. “No one should take for granted the right to vote to begin with, and the right to vote secretly,” said Handschu, an artist and representative for Detroit Advocates of the Blind. “Those are pretty important rights of citizenship. And what can I say? I wish we didn’t have to fuss so long to get here, but I’m delighted we got here. And at least today for me, the system did work.” Stephen Handschu, a Detroit artist and representative for Detroit Advocates of the Blind, voted at the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Handschu was among the residents who spoke out before City Council last month about concerns with voting equipment for residents with disabilities. Credit: Bryce Huffman, BridgeDetroit Handschu’s voting experience comes after he and others appealed to Detroit’s City Council about struggles at the polls often endured by the disabled community, including what they have said is a lack of training for VAT setup and use that sometimes resulted in an hourslong ordeal or prevented Detroiters with disabilities from being able to vote without assistance. “At least today for me, the system did work,” he told BridgeDetroit after casting his ballot. Handschu walked from his home on the other side of Grand Circus Park and up to the fourth floor of the church Tuesday, he said, because he had to fill out extra paperwork to vote in-person since he’d first submitted an absentee ballot and had to void that submission. The ballot was long, he said, and using the VAT was “cumbersome,” he told BridgeDetroit. “The voting process took nearly two hours I believe for me, which I think is excessive,” he said. “But having said those little minor things, the machine worked this time, and I’m very very happy that it worked. And, I got to vote secretly and independently.” The clerk’s office has faced accessibility questions ahead of the 2025 city election, in 2024 and in 2022. The nonprofit advocacy group Detroit Disability Power has conducted multiple surveys of polling sites. Last year, the group found there were widespread barriers to accessibility, including entrances and doorways, with 70% of the individuals surveyed reporting problems with VATs. The Detroit Department of Elections previously told BridgeDetroit there is a Voter Assistance Terminal at all of the city’s 158 polling locations. There are also additional machines in reserve that can be used as needed. The department added that complaints about VATs aren’t made often. But when they are received, a team is quickly dispatched to the polling site to rectify it. The team either resolves the issue with the machine or replaces it with one of the department’s VAT reserves. Handschu said in the past there have been multiple roadblocks, including nonfunctioning machines, missing earphones and volume issues. But today, those problems were there. “I don’t want to say everything’s fine for everybody because I’m just one person and I only have my experience,” he said. “But … I got to cast my vote secretly, and that’s what I was looking for.” 12:15 p.m. — Tuesday, Nov. 3 Southwest Detroit voters at the polls voiced concern over financial hardship and rising costs as they shared their hopes that the Nov. 3 election could signal a shift in policy change. Within the groups of people at Mayberry Elementary casting their votes was brother and sister duo Henry McCoi and Cynthia Linger. McCoi, an 80-year-old retiree, said even though Republican President Donald Trump is not on the midterm ballot, Trump was his primary motivation to cast his vote for Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson. “I voted to go against Trump. When it all comes down to it, we are trying to vote against Trump,” McCoi said. McCoi said that the state of the economy under Trump’s second administration has made it so he cannot afford his costs of living on his Social Security benefits alone. “I have to limit myself, cut different areas like my gasoline or my electricity or my water or my phone, just to survive,” McCoi said. For Linger, 88, casting her straight Democratic ticket in person on Tuesday was a matter of principle. “As an American citizen I wanted to vote for the people I feel will do much more for Michigan,” Linger said. “My right to vote is my right to speak for what I want and what I expect.” Nichelle Williams, a southwest Detroit home healthcare worker, said it was crucial to cast her vote at Mayberry Elementary on Tuesday for Democratic candidates that she hopes can slow federal cuts to food assistance programs. “We need a change in the economy and direction things are going,” Williams said. “People can’t afford to live day to day and they just keep taking away food stamps.” Williams, 33, has a freshman daughter at University Preparatory Academy, and said that while she wasn’t familiar with the dozens of candidates for the board of the Detroit Public Schools Community District she feels it is time to “shake things up.” She cited the district’s long-running struggles with literacy rates. A $94.4 million settlement gave DPSCD the resources it needed to hire hundreds of academic interventionists to work with struggling students. Flights across Europe searched and diverted after hoax bomb threats
articles.description: Flights across Europe searched and diverted after hoax bomb threats AP News Seven reported bomb threats against European flights confirmed as false alarms – as it happened The Guardian Seven planes searched after suspected bomb threats across Europe BBC Bomb threats cause flight disruptions across Europe Reuters Hoax bomb threats target four European flights as scares spread across the continent Euronews.com
articles.content: BERLIN (AP) — Several flights across Europe received hoax bomb threats Tuesday that prompted searches, diversions and, in one case, an escort by the Italian Air Force until landing, officials said. The flights included Polish airline LOT, Scandinavian Airlines, Wizz Air and Ryanair. The hoax threats came a day after a plane headed for Bulgaria was diverted to Hungary after receiving a similar bomb threat while in the air. No one was injured. Matthew Borie of Osprey Flight Solutions, which advises airlines on flight threats, gave several hypotheses for the as-yet unexplained incidents: A single threat triggers copycat incidents; an individual or a group makes multiple threats; or operations of “hybrid warfare” by state actors or their supporters. Such threats were “not a new phenomenon” and came at a time of increased geopolitical tensions and signs of “disruption,” like attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems, drone incursions in Europe and mysterious triggers to alert apps — even as authorities have warned that hybrid threats abound. The focus on Europe means “there could be a Russian angle,” said Borie, the company’s co-founder and chief intelligence officer. “We need to keep in mind, though, that Iranian hybrid warfare is just as active in certain pockets of Europe as well.” His message for travelers? “Don’t be alarmed,” he said, noting “coordinated response mechanisms” by national authorities — including, at times, the deployment of NATO fighter jets to escort such planes. A Ryanair flight from Lisbon landed in Rome’s Fiumicino airport Tuesday morning after receipt of an email reporting a bomb was on board, according to information provided by a Fiumicino official with knowledge of the events. Police bomb disposal experts carried out security checks of passengers, crew and baggage and found no explosives. There was also a bomb threat reported on another Ryanair flight to Rome from Dublin, with no explosives found, the official said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly. The Italian Air Force confirmed it scrambled two Air Force Eurofighters to “intercept and escort” a plane bound for Rome. It said it responded immediately “following a report of a suspected threat aboard a civilian aircraft flying from Dublin to Rome Fiumicino.” In Poland, meanwhile, a morning flight by Polish airline LOT from London’s Heathrow Airport to Warsaw’s main Chopin Airport was diverted to nearby Modlin Airport after a bomb threat, Polish press agency PAP reported. Modlin Airport was closed temporarily. LOT said “nothing was found on the aircraft” after a search of the jet at Modlin. Airport officials said normal airport operations had resumed. They did not give further details on the nature of the threats. Chopin Airport also received information about a potentially dangerous item on board a Scandinavian Airlines, or SAS, flight inbound from Copenhagen, PAP reported. The airport’s communications office told the news agency that standard safety procedures were immediately implemented, and one of the airport’s runways was closed. “The passengers disembarked, the plane landed normally; it was not an emergency landing,” SAS spokesperson Alexandra Lindgren Kaoukji told PAP. She said the matter has been referred to the Polish police. Spanish officials on Tuesday ruled out the presence of explosives on a Ryanair plane from Manchester that landed in southern Spain’s Murcia Airport following a bomb threat. Passengers and crew went through a security check, and the aircraft was inspected, said Francisco Lucas, the Spanish government’s delegate in the Murcia region, on X. The flight had 121 people on board, including crew, he said. Bulgarian authorities found no signs of explosives on two aircraft at the Sofia International Airport that had both received bomb threats Tuesday while en route, Bulgaria’s Minister of Transportation Georgi Peev said on Tuesday, according to state news agency BTA. The two planes, originating in Bergamo, Italy, and Dublin, Ireland, were inspected by counter-terrorism officers after landing in Sofia. Neither had been diverted due to the bomb threats. Peev said that the initial information on the existence of one of the bomb threats “was based on a report from the pilot.” “The pilot received information through his own channels — from the airline — that such a threat existed,” Peev said, adding that Bulgarian air traffic control then followed a protocol for such threats that landed the aircraft safely in Sofia. The bomb threats came a day after a Wizz Air flight that departed Luton Airport near London was forced to divert to Hungary after a bomb threat received while the plane was in the air. Hungarian Defense Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said in a Facebook post on Monday that a Gripen fighter jet from the Hungarian Air Force was scrambled to intercept the Wizz Air flight and escorted it safely to the Liszt Ferenc International Airport in Budapest. Authorities found no threat aboard the aircraft after conducting an inspection of the plane and its passengers, Wizz Air told state news agency MTI. On Tuesday, Bulgaria’s acting Interior Ministry Secretary General Lyubomir Nikolov told reporters that authorities were still trying to identify the sender of the threat. Last month, a flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna made an emergency landing in Bulgaria following a bomb threat. Greek authorities were investigating a bomb threat against a Panamanian-flagged, Israeli-run cruise ship in the port of the Aegean island of Syros. No suspicious objects were found in Tuesday’s initial search of the cruise ship, the Crown Iris, by coast guard officers with a sniffer dog and a diver, and a specialist diving unit was on its way to conduct further checks, the coast guard said. The ship, which had been scheduled to sail for Haifa in Israel with 940 passengers and 597 crew on board, was being evacuated as a precaution, the coast guard added. The presence of the Crown Iris in Greek ports has triggered protests in the past, mainly from activists opposing the war in Gaza. Biller reported from Rome. Associated Press journalists Elena Becatoros in Athens, Greece; Suman Naishadham in Madrid; Jamey Keaten in Geneva; and Justin Spike in Budapest, Hungary, contributed to this report.

articles.content: AMD CEO Lisa Su said in the company’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday that Q3 2026 was “was the largest and most profitable in our history.” AMD reported a record $13.4 billion in quarterly revenue, and it’s predicting it will hit another record high next quarter of $17 billion. The company’s data center business is driving that growth, with $8.5 billion in data center quarterly revenue for Q3 2026. Su said AMD’s expecting its revenue to “grow more than 80 percent in 2027,” adding that “data center will be the largest contributor.” Eventually, most of AMD’s revenue might come from its data center business. In response to a question during Tuesday’s earnings call, CFO Jean Hu said, “Looking ahead of 2027, we actually think our data center business will be more than 80 percent of total company revenue.” As of Q3 2026, roughly 63 percent of AMD’s net quarterly revenue was from its data center business. Over the last couple years, jumps in the company’s revenue have been closely mirroring its data center business — in Q3 2026 its overall revenue went up $1.9 billion, while its data center revenue went up $1.8 billion. As AMD keeps smashing its data center revenue records, its gaming business dropped 40 percent compared to last year, dipping to $773 million. PCs, game consoles, and other tech have been hit with price hikes over recent months due to shortages of RAM and other components, driven by demand from AI data centers. articles.description: WASHINGTON — In a stunning upset, Democrats ousted Republicans and flipped control of the U.S. Senate Tuesday night, effectively establishing a barricade for President Donald Trump’s agenda for the last two years of his term. Democrats will now have the power to block many of Trump’s nominees, both executive and judicial, including if a spot […]
articles.content: Michigan's 2026 race for U.S. Senate was one of the most watched in the nation. In this photo, voters wait in line outside the Department of Elections in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)WASHINGTON — In a stunning upset, Democrats ousted Republicans and flipped control of the U.S. Senate Tuesday night, effectively establishing a barricade for President Donald Trump’s agenda for the last two years of his term. Democrats will now have the power to block many of Trump’s nominees, both executive and judicial, including if a spot opens on the U.S. Supreme Court bench. The decisive rebuke of Trump became apparent just after 11:30 p.m. Eastern, when The Associated Press called the Iowa Senate race for Democrat Josh Turek, who clinched the open seat over Republican candidate Ashley Hinson. Voters increasingly grew dissatisfied as the midterms approached with high gas and diesel prices, and overall inflation, driven up by Trump’s stalled war in Iran and erratic tariff policies. The economic woes, which also include increasing food prices and skyrocketing healthcare costs, hung over Republican candidates as they campaigned in recent months. Trump immediately posted on Truth Social, “I’m going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!” During a live phone interview with Fox News just after midnight Wednesday, Trump chalked up the widespread losses to him not being on the ballot and to high gas prices. “If I was on the ballot, they would have gotten out. Look, they got out for the rallies. You never saw rallies that big,” he told the Fox hosts. When asked whether he thought the prolonged war in Iran factored into the results, he said, “I don’t think it’s the war.” “I think it’s the gasoline prices. People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline. And that you know, I understand that,” he said. He ended the relatively brief call by congratulating the Democrats. “Well, I say this: congratulations to the Democrats. They did a good job. They’ve been looking for this one for 11 years, and they finally got it. But I don’t view it as a hit on me. I think we’ve done a, we’ve had the greatest two years in the history of the presidency in terms of the economy, in terms of all the things that we’ve done.” Earlier in the evening a White House official said on background that Trump’s mood remained “defiant.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called the results Tuesday night “a generational remake of the Senate map.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune said his party will continue “to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism.” In an early morning post on X, the South Dakota Republican touted Republicans’ “strong record of accomplishments,” citing closing the southern border and passing tax cuts, among other items. “As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done,” he wrote. Kansas shocker A political earthquake rattled Kansas, where Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton sailed past incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, marking the first time Kansans have elected a Democrat in nearly a century. Marshall, an OB-GYN, had released his closing argument Sunday in a brief video during which he defended his former medical practice for sending clients who carried unpaid balances to collection agencies. Speaking directly to the camera, Marshall said during the one-minute ad, “To ensure that 40,000 Kansans would still have access to care, we did have to keep the lights on. So we occasionally handed some accounts over to a collection agency, just like nearly every private medical practice does.” The issue had dogged Marshall’s campaign since the New York Times reported in September that the Kansas doctor had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with unpaid bills. Patients were arrested in 81 of the cases for missing court dates. The patients filed a class action lawsuit against Marshall Thursday, Kansas Reflector reported. In Iowa, Democratic state legislator Turek defeated Hinson, a GOP member of the U.S. House, to win the open Senate seat — delivering another massive setback for Republicans. Turek will now be the first Democratic senator to represent Iowa in more than a decade. The two-time Paralympic gold medalist and state representative received an early endorsement in July from former President Barack Obama. The two appeared in a campaign ad playing basketball. Iowa was Trump’s next-to-last in-person campaign stop on his whirlwind schedule to support midterm candidates in several reliably Republican states. Upsets all over the map In a major upset, Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat, won the Senate race in South Carolina, defeating Republican Sen. Darline Graham. Graham had been appointed in July to serve out the remainder of her late brother Lindsey Graham’s term. Andrews will be the first Democratic senator to represent South Carolina in more than 20 years. Texas voters also delivered another staggering upset in electing Democrat James Talarico by a wide margin over Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. The flip of deep red Texas to blue signified a major blow for Trump, who backed Paxton in the GOP primary over four-term Sen. John Cornyn. Paxton, who has served as Texas attorney general since 2015, was impeached by the Texas House in May 2023 on charges of bribery, disregard of duties and several other articles of impeachment. The Texas Senate acquitted Paxton of all charges the following September. Paxton was indicted on state fraud charges in 2015. He reached a $300,000 settlement deal to end the state probe in 2024. Veteran Republican senator ousted In an early-morning statement, longtime Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins conceded her Senate seat to a newcomer, Democrat Troy Jackson. Collins called her nearly 30-year run in the Senate “the honor of my life.” Jackson entered the race as a late candidate after the Democrats’ initial choice, Graham Platner, ended his campaign in July following multiple allegations of sexual assault. Jackson was mobbed by national press at his final campaign stop in South Portland. He told reporters he’s very hopeful given “the amount of people turning out, the way things are going, the way people are talking.” “In the end, people want change and I think people see me as a change candidate, for what’s going on in this country, I feel really good about it, I really do.” In North Carolina, in yet another upset that had been predicted in polling, Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper won the Senate race in the Tar Heel State, flipping the open seat held by retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. Cooper had faced GOP candidate Michael Whatley, who previously chaired the Republican National Committee and the North Carolina Republican Party. Tillis announced in June 2025 he would not seek reelection after Trump vowed to primary him because he voted “no” on the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” the president’s major tax and spending cuts package. In the Buckeye State, Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown won his Senate seat back, defeating incumbent GOP Sen. Jon Husted in another major upset for Republicans. Brown spent 18 years in the Senate but lost his reelection bid in 2024 to Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. Husted’s seat was formerly held by Vice President JD Vance before Vance was elected on the Republican presidential ticket with Trump in 2024. Trump and Vance headlined multiple rallies throughout Ohio in support of Husted. Trump’s campaign stops for Husted drew attention last month for his repeated remarks about Husted’s physical appearance, with a focus on his backside. More races Democratic Sen. Mark Warner retained his seat in Virginia, according to a race call by The Associated Press just after 7 p.m. Eastern. Georgia Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff also kept his Senate seat, the AP called shortly before 8 p.m. Eastern. Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Ed Markey also kept his Senate spot, the AP called, as did Democratic Sens. Jack Reed of Rhode Island, Chris Coons of Delaware, Cory Booker of New Jersey, John Hickenlooper of Colorado, Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Jeff Merkley of Oregon. Juliana Stratton, a Democrat, also won the Senate race in Illinois. In Minnesota, Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat, won her Senate bid, AP called early Wednesday. New Hampshire Democrat Chris Pappas won the Senate race there, keeping a seat that was held by Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the AP called. Pappas ran against Republican John Sununu. Republican seats In Florida, incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody pulled ahead of Democratic candidate Angie Nixon, according to an AP race call, after precincts in the Florida panhandle tallied results. The race between Moody and the progressive state representative was unexpectedly close in the Republican stronghold. Progressives flocked to Florida to stump for Nixon, including independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Democratic U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York City. Nixon’s platform was closely aligned with but not identical to the national Democratic Socialists of America. West Virginia GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito won the Senate race in the Mountain State, AP called shortly before 9 p.m. Eastern. In another expected win for the GOP, Wyoming Republican U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman cruised to victory for a seat in the upper chamber. Kentucky GOP U.S. Rep. Andy Barr won his Senate race in the Bluegrass State, AP called. In Oklahoma, Republican U.S. Rep. Kevin Hern won a Senate seat in the reliably red state. In Arkansas, GOP Sen. Tom Cotton won his Senate race, AP called. Alabama GOP U.S. Rep. Barry Moore won his Senate bid in the ruby red state. In Tennessee, Republican Sen. Bill Hagerty won his Senate race. In South Dakota, GOP Sen. Mike Rounds won his Senate race, AP called early Wednesday. In Louisiana, GOP U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow won her Senate bid in the Pelican State. In Idaho, Republican Sen. Jim Risch was reelected. Ahead of Election Day, the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter had identified close contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. Trump’s Republican party vied to hold on to its narrow majority in the House and maintain control in the Senate, where the party currently holds 53 Senate seats. Tuesday’s results delivered Democrats the majority in the upper chamber. Here’s a closer look at some of the remaining hotly contested races: Alaska Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is up against incumbent GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska. Trump’s Department of Justice preemptively sued the state’s election officials to try to block them from certifying the Senate election results if Dan S. Sullivan loses by a smaller margin than the number of votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan. A federal judge in Alaska dismissed the case Sunday, citing the federal government’s failure to explain how it had the authority to bring the case. Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy was challenged earlier in the year in state court, and Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled in June he could remain on the ballot. The Trump administration vowed to appeal. The New York Times reported Oct. 28 that Democratic operatives recruited Dan J. Sullivan to be a spoiler candidate. States Newsroom has not independently verified the allegations. Peltola denied any knowledge of the alleged scheme, according to Alaska Beacon.
