articles.title: Democrats win sizable US House majority amid sweep of close races
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Democrats will regain control of the U.S. House early next year, after voters throughout the country rejected the policies that Republicans and President Donald Trump implemented during the last two years. The Associated Press, which States Newsroom looks to for the projected winner of congressional races, called the House for Democrats early Wednesday […]
articles.content: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., greets volunteers during a midterm election night watch party with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 3, 2026. Democrats anticipate flipping Republican control of the U.S. House. (Tom Brenner/Getty Images)WASHINGTON — Democrats will regain control of the U.S. House early next year, after voters throughout the country rejected the policies that Republicans and President Donald Trump implemented during the last two years. The Associated Press, which States Newsroom looks to for the projected winner of congressional races, called the House for Democrats early Wednesday morning after the party passed the 218-seat threshold. While there are still some close races without a declared winner, the latest unofficial results show both the House and Senate will flip to Democratic majorities in early January when the next session of Congress begins. Democrats are on track to have at least 224 lawmakers in the House and a minimum of 53 in the Senate, giving them considerable negotiating leverage with Trump, if he chooses to broker bipartisan agreements. Trump, who was watching the returns from the White House, wrote in a social media post that he wasn’t responsible for the Republican losses. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter,” he wrote. Trump later posted an image of a red baseball cap with the word “VETO” embroidered into it, indicating he may not be open to working with Democrats despite the signal voters sent. New York Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the first Black speaker, celebrated late Tuesday night as early returns showed the party was poised to flip that chamber of Congress. “The American people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,” he said. “They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January.” Democrats, he said, understand voters expect the party to “deliver dramatic change” to help people struggling with the rising cost of living. Jeffries also pledged to “bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption on this country.” “Because if you have people in high office who are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends, or their donors, then they’re not focused on making life better for the American people,” he said. Louisiana Republican Rep. Mike Johnson, the current speaker, wrote in a statement that “the American people have made the same decision that has been made in all but two midterms in the last century.” “While the outcome of this midterm is not what we’d hoped and fought for, a new battle is just beginning,” Johnson wrote. “This Democrat House majority will be led by the most radical and extreme leftists in American history. However, Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect the foundations that have made America the greatest nation in the history of the world.” Democrats are likely to launch a series of investigations — and possibly impeachment proceedings — into the president and members of his administration. The simmering tension between the two parties is only projected to grow amid divided government, but Republicans and Democrats will need to work together on issues like government funding if they want to avoid more record-setting shutdowns. Republicans have so far lost a total of 25 seats to Democrats, including some that were considered safe for GOP candidates. California’s 1st district, where state Sen. Mike McGuire defeated Republican incumbent James Gallagher. California’s 3rd district went to incumbent Democratic Rep. Ami Bera, who was redistricted after the state redrew lines to favor Democrats. California’s 41st district went to incumbent Democratic Rep. Linda Sánchez, who was redistricted after the state redrew lines to favor Democrats. Colorado’s 8th district, where former state Rep. Manny Rutinel beat GOP incumbent Gabe Evans. In Indiana’s 5th district, Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democratic candidate J.D. Ford. Iowa’s 1st district went to Democratic candidate Christina Bohannan, who beat incumbent Rep. Mariannette Miller‑Meeks. In Iowa’s 2nd district, Democratic candidate Lindsay James beat GOP candidate Joe Mitchell. Iowa’s 3rd district went to Democratic candidate Sarah Trone Garriott, who won against GOP incumbent Zach Nunn. Kentucky’s 6th district, where former Assistant U.S. Attorney Zach Dembo, a Democrat, won. Missouri’s 2nd district went to Democratic candidate Fred Wellman, who defeated Rep. Ann Wagner. Nebraska’s 2nd district, where Democratic candidate Denise Powell defeated GOP candidate Brinker Harding. Both were vying for the seat by retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon, a moderate Republican who is a frequent critic of the president. Republican Rep. Thomas Kean Jr. lost his reelection bid in New Jersey’s 17th district after he missed more than 100 votes from March to June, which he attributed to depression he was undergoing treatment for. North Carolina Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards lost after he suspended his reelection campaign following an ethics complaint of inappropriate behavior toward female staffers. In Ohio’s 7th district, Rep Max Miller lost his reelection. Ohio’s 15th district, where Democratic candidate Don Leonard defeated Republican incumbent Mike Carey. Four were in Pennsylvania. Incumbents Ryan Mackenzie of district 7 and Rob Bresnahan of district 8, who flipped their districts in 2024 lost. Scott Perry, who was seeking an eighth term, also lost his reelection. In district 1, GOP incumbent Brian Fitzpatrick lost to Democratic candidate Bob Harvie. In Texas’ 15th district, Tejano musician and Democratic candidate Bobby Pulido defeated GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz. In the 23rd district of Texas, Democratic candidate Katy Padilla Stout defeated Republican candidate Brandon Herrera. Utah’s 1st district went to Democratic candidate Ben McAdams who defeated GOP candidate Riley Owen. In Virginia’s 2nd district, GOP incumbent Jen A. Kiggans lost to Democratic candidate Elaine G. Luria. Wisconsin’s 1st district went to Democratic candidate Mitchell Berman, who defeated GOP Rep. Bryan Steil. In Wisconsin’s 3rd district, Democratic candidate Rebecca Cooke beat GOP incumbent Derrick Van Orden. Jonathan Shorman contributed to this report.

articles.title: Voters sail through a mostly smooth Election Day, despite fears of federal interference
articles.description: America voted. After the Trump administration pressured election officials, after concerns that armed federal agents would deploy to the polls, after fears U.S. Department of Justice election monitors would intimidate voters — ballots were cast by the millions Tuesday, mostly without incident. Across the United States, voters headed to their polling places. At churches, schools and […]
articles.content: Poll workers wait for voters at a polling place in a garage on Willett Road in Brentwood, Pennsylvania, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)America voted. After the Trump administration pressured election officials, after concerns that armed federal agents would deploy to the polls, after fears U.S. Department of Justice election monitors would intimidate voters — ballots were cast by the millions Tuesday, mostly without incident. Across the United States, voters headed to their polling places. At churches, schools and community centers, they rendered their verdict on the direction of the country and those who lead it. As the votes are counted, what comes next is uncertain. President Donald Trump has long put forward false allegations of election fraud and baseless conspiracy theories to undermine results he doesn’t like. Democrats appeared well on their way to retaking control of Congress as votes were counted Tuesday night, ushering in a new era of divided government in Washington, D.C. Trump didn’t immediately allege fraud as the scale of GOP losses began to come into focus. On social media late Tuesday, Trump wrote that if he had been on the ballot, “we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Days or weeks of courtroom battles could lie ahead if Trump deploys the machinery of the federal government to advance claims of a stolen election. His 2020 election loss set off a host of unsuccessful lawsuits that tried to overturn election results in battleground states, part of a campaign that culminated in a mob of his supporters storming the Capitol. But on Tuesday, American democracy passed a crucial test — voters voted. “What we’re seeing today could have looked a lot different,” Andrew Walchuk, policy director and counsel for the nonpartisan watchdog group Common Cause, told reporters. “We could have seen a lot of different scenarios based on what the administration wanted to get away with.” Over the past year, the Trump administration filed dozens of election-related lawsuits on everything from voter rolls to ballot counting. Federal courts halted nearly all of these efforts, including a demand that California set aside the ballots of 20,000 people the Trump administration alleged were suspected noncitizens. Trump and his allies have said they’re focused on preventing noncitizen voting, which they say cancels out the votes of U.S. citizens. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has arrested dozens of alleged noncitizen voters in recent weeks, and the president continues to call on Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require voters to prove their citizenship. “We are going to continue our yearslong fight on Election Integrity,” Trump wrote in a Saturday social media post. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued multiple warnings against illegal voting on Tuesday. On social media he wrote that if ineligible voters cast a ballot, DHS “will find you, hunt you down, and you will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” In the states Whatever happens next, on Tuesday states administered elections under their own rules as laid out in the U.S. Constitution. In Albuquerque, New Mexico, Jolyne Marshall, who said her top priority was “stopping the descent into fascism,” said she had heard talk about the potential for voter suppression, such as federal agents at polling places. On Tuesday, she said she had a seamless voting experience. The Rev. Suzanne Parker Miller spent Election Day as a poll chaplain in Raleigh, North Carolina, for Faith United to Save Democracy, a nonpartisan, multi-faith group. She said she had been told to anticipate some type of federal presence in the area. “I didn’t know what to expect today, which is just always a little unnerving,” Parker Miller said. “But I’ve done this in the past and what I came in expecting today was to also have a very peaceful and fair and free election.” The Justice Department deployed about 1,000 election monitors across the country and in addition to DOJ personnel, drew upon federal law enforcement agents typically not assigned to the polls. The makeup of the monitors raised concerns among Democrats and voting rights leaders that they could be used to intimidate voters. The Michigan Department of Attorney General said it was following up on reports that monitors in Flint had improperly asked poll workers about the details of their training and in Dearborn had asked for copies of training materials. State officials said they had contacted the Justice Department’s election monitor coordinator for Michigan about the activity. “That coordinator confirmed that this activity that the monitors were engaging in is not consistent with how the monitors were trained,” Angela Benander, a spokesperson for the Michigan Department of State, told reporters. Leaders with the League of Women Voters in Ohio and Pennsylvania said during a news conference that monitors in their states were wearing plain clothes and staying out of the way. “They’re really just asking short questions of voters when they come out, sometimes,” Jen Miller, executive director of the League of Women Voters of Ohio, told reporters. Usual election problems Across the country, election officials said the challenges they encountered on Tuesday centered on typical problems — the weather, power outages and technical issues — and not federal interference. The most significant problem appeared in Westchester County, New York, where voting machines were unable to accept paper ballots. The New York State Board of Elections said in a statement that an update to the county’s election programming caused the issue. Election officials emphasized that voting continued and that ballots were being kept in secure bags, though the problem could affect the speed of results. The area includes the district of Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, who faces Democrat Cait Conley in a closely watched toss-up race. Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins, a Democrat, said in a statement that the county had fallen short of the standard of providing a fair, secure and seamless election process. He promised to convene a bipartisan team to review the decisions and failures that led to “this debacle.” “The voters deserve better, and I intend to make sure they get it,” Jenkins said. Lawsuit after lawsuit Despite isolated problems, the relative smoothness of voting across the country stood in stark contrast to the frenetic pace of legal challenges that played out in the months, days and hours before Tuesday. As Election Day approached, the Justice Department sued Alaska and California. In Alaska, the Trump administration sought to preemptively pause certification of the U.S. Senate election, an effort a federal judge quickly dismissed. In California, Justice Department lawyers raised the possibility that election officials could face prosecution if they tabulated the ballots of noncitizens. A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from issuing threats, but that order was halted Tuesday by an en banc panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals — a rare election-related legal victory for the president. “The rule of law prevails. Separation of powers does not allow judges to take control of core executive branch powers. We will conduct our criminal investigations without fear or favor,” Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote on social media. The Justice Department alleged in a lawsuit that Homeland Security had identified 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters registered in the state. It demanded California set aside the ballots of anyone on the list. State and local election officials raised concerns about the accuracy of the list and said the demand encroached on their authority over elections. A district court judge and an appeals court both rejected the demand. And on Monday, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request in a one-sentence order that election legal experts said spoke volumes. In a statement, the Justice Department said it was disappointed in the decision but that the court loss wasn’t the end of its efforts. In addition to deploying monitors and charging noncitizen voters, the department said it would “pursue other legal avenues to ensure that only eligible American citizens vote.” David Becker, a former Justice Department Voting Section attorney who leads the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, on a press call noted that the Supreme Court had issued its order without any dissents or explanation. “Just a complete smackdown,” Becker said, adding that the justices were sending a message that “they’re not going to credit any future efforts to impose federal fiat on the states as they manage their elections.” Joshua Bowling of Source New Mexico, Clayton Henkel of NC Newsline and Jon King of Michigan Advance contributed reporting.

articles.title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
articles.description: Called FlashProve, the system would let anyone check that an AI response really came from the model it claims to be from.
articles.content: Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday. The system, called FlashProve, is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model. It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using. Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model. In particular, the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results. FlashProve could also be used to verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model. “A developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model,” the researchers write. “How can a user verify these claims?” To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a “fingerprint” of each model they release that can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. Crucially, the fingerprints don’t reveal a model’s weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. That means labs could publish the fingerprints without giving up their most valuable asset, enabling the system to work with commercial models, too. The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device. As part of the announcement, researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub. Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab. “This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda,” researchers explain in the announcement post. “We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.content: Voters wait in line on Nov. 3, 2026, at Bethlehem Lutheran Church in Lansing, Mich., one of several local polling places in Ingham County. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Michigan election officials say they contacted the U.S. Department of Justice on Tuesday after receiving reports that federal election monitors in Dearborn and Flint had questioned poll workers about their training, conduct which state officials said was outside the monitors’ legal authority. Kim Bush, a spokeswoman for Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, said DOJ monitors in Dearborn asked poll workers for copies of their training materials, while monitors in Flint asked questions about how poll workers were trained. The Michigan Department of State and Attorney General’s Office contacted the DOJ’s Michigan election monitor coordinator, who acknowledged the reported conduct was inconsistent with the monitors’ training and said the department would speak directly with monitors to clarify what they are permitted to do. “That coordinator confirmed that this activity that the monitors were engaging in is not consistent with how the monitors were trained. and that they would follow up with the monitors on the ground in Dearborn to remind them of what they are not permitted to do and what they are permitted to do,” Angela Benander, spokesperson for the department of state, told reporters. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE A request for comment was sent by Michigan Advance to the DOJ, but has yet to be returned. This story will be updated when a response is received. Under Michigan law, DOJ monitors are generally limited to observing election procedures. They cannot question poll workers about their training or handle election materials. They also cannot enter a polling location without permission from the local clerk. State officials said they had also received reports of DOJ monitors speaking with voters in Lansing but had no concerns about those interactions. The law permits monitors to speak with voters outside polling locations after they have cast their ballots, provided voters are told they are not required to participate, which the monitors reportedly did. As of Tuesday afternoon, state officials said they had received no additional reports of concerning conduct by DOJ or congressional election observers and had not identified any significant problems beyond routine Election Day issues, such as equipment malfunctions. “We have, it sounds like, pretty consistently high turnout,” Benander said during a 3 p.m. briefing. “But at this time, the report that we have to share is that things are running smoothly.” Seventy-one DOJ monitors were assigned to polling locations in Detroit, Dearborn, Hamtramck, East Lansing, Grand Rapids, Flint and Warren.

articles.description: Cybersecurity-focused Ballistic Ventures is seeking to raise $360 million for a new flagship fund and another $130 million for a separate investment vehicle.
articles.content: Ballistic Ventures, the cybersecurity-focused venture capital firm co-founded by former Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein (pictured above, second from the right), is seeking to raise $490 million across two new funds, TechCrunch has learned through regulatory filings. The San Francisco-based VC firm filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission this week to raise $360 million for its third flagship fund, matching the size of its previous fund raised in 2024, and another $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund B. Neither fund had recorded any sales at the time of filing. The fundraising plans come as the growing use of artificial intelligence has raised concerns about more sophisticated cyberattacks. The rise of AI agents has also created new opportunities for cybersecurity startups and the venture capital firms backing them. Founded in late 2021, Ballistic Ventures’ founding team includes Schlein, former AT&T Cybersecurity president Barmak Meftah, and Roger Thornton, who co-founded security companies Fortify Software and AlienVault. The firm has backed companies, including Talon Cyber Security, acquired by Palo Alto Networks, and Pangea, bought by CrowdStrike, alongside startups such as Armadin, GetReal, Nudge Security, and Oligo Security. Ballistic’s ties to storied venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins, where Schlein spent more than two decades, help set it apart from rivals, a cybersecurity investor at another VC firm told TechCrunch. Its investment strategy, however, is similar to those of other cybersecurity-focused investors, including Forgepoint Capital and Ten Eleven Ventures, the person said. In 2022, Ballistic announced its $300 million debut fund and raised another $360 million for its second flagship fund two years later. It also raised about $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund A, per PitchBook data. The new Fund B is targeting a similar amount. U.S. cybersecurity startups raised $11.5 billion in 2025, the highest since 2022, a recent report by JPMorgan Chase said, citing PitchBook data. AI-enabled companies accounted for about 72% of U.S. cybersecurity venture deals through May this year, compared with 36% in 2019, the report said. Separately, Microsoft, in its annual Digital Defense Report released last month, warned that hackers are increasingly using AI for activities ranging from phishing and social engineering to malware development. The technology is allowing attackers to operate faster and at greater scale, even as many of their underlying techniques remain unchanged. Ballistic Ventures declined to comment on its fundraising plans. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. articles.title: Detroit turnout takes center stage as voters weigh Michigan’s US Senate race
articles.description: DETROIT— Despite backlash from Democratic lawmakers over U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, Detroit-area voters say the move only reinforced their support for Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Aijah Greer, 27, of Detroit told Michigan Advance that it did more good than harm for Democrats and that El-Sayed […]
articles.content: Voters wait in line outside the Department of Elections in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)DETROIT— Despite backlash from Democratic lawmakers over U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, Detroit-area voters say the move only reinforced their support for Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Aijah Greer, 27, of Detroit told Michigan Advance that it did more good than harm for Democrats and that El-Sayed should thank Stevens if he wins. “It was a poor decision on her part,” Greer said. “She should have stuck with where she was at instead of switching over, especially so late in the race.” Greer listed gas prices, housing, healthcare and education as her biggest concerns. “What he’s doing aligns with all the changes I want to see. Mike Rogers is not really for us and I feel like Abdul is more for us, the people,” she said. The endorsement sent shockwaves through the party. State and federal lawmakers condemned Stevens, calling her decision “despicable” and a betrayal. Stevens had initially endorsed El-Sayed after losing to him in the Democratic primary. Shortly after she endorsed Rogers, Curtis Hertel Jr., chair of the Michigan Democratic Party, announced in a social media post that Stevens was no longer a member of the party. “I can’t stop her from running as a Democrat but she will have no tools with the Democratic Party moving forward,” Hertel told Don Lemon in an interview on Monday. By the time Stevens endorsed Rogers on Sunday, more than 2.3 million Michigan residents had already voted either by mail or at an early voting site, according to Michigan’s Department of State. That number had grown to over 2.5 million by 1 p.m. Tuesday. High voter turnout in Detroit is seen as integral to success for Democratic candidates, especially El-Sayed. Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey said she expected between 100,000 and 130,000 voters to cast ballots at their polling locations . “Voting is the heart of democracy and we need everyone in the city of Detroit and in the state of Michigan to participate in the process today,” Winfrey told reporters late Tuesday morning. Winfrey expected turnout to be at about 45%, which would beat 2018’s 42% rate. Election workers collect absentee ballots outside the Department of Elections in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance) Richard Newell of Highland Park also cited the rising cost of living as one of his biggest concerns. It was the 80-year-old’s first time voting. “As it stands now, groceries and gas are literally robbing the people,” Newell said. “The Republican Party, as I see it, they’re just terrorizing the community.” He called Stevens’ endorsement a “betrayal” but that it made him more excited to vote for El-Sayed. “He’s a medical professional, he has an empathetic heart and I think his concerns are in the right place,” he said. Newell also found it touching when El-Sayed spoke about his daughters, especially because youth violence is another one of his concerns. “There’s a lot of peer pressure,” he said. “If you don’t hurt somebody or you aren’t in a gang, you’re considered an outsider and I think we need more focus on younger people coming up because it’s deplorable.” Another first-time voter, Airyana Davis of Detroit, described her experience as exciting but nerve racking. “There’s a first time for everything,” the 19-year-old said. She encouraged other people her age to make their voices heard by voting.

Michigan officials report issues with tabulators, election monitors
articles.content: LANSING — Ballot tabulators malfunctioned at various places around the state and there were at least two instances in which election monitors from the U.S. Department of Justice overstepped their authority on Election Day, officials said Nov. 3. Malfunctioning tabulators delayed some voting in Redford Township, Shelby Township and Madison Heights, as well as other locations, officials said. And there were two instances, in Dearborn and in Flint, in which DOJ monitors communicated with election workers in ways they shouldn't have, said Kimberly Bush, a spokesperson for the Michigan Attorney General's Office. In Dearborn, monitors asked election workers for copies of their training materials and, in Flint, monitors asked election workers questions about their training, Bush said. In both cases, Michigan officials contacted the DOJ, who confirmed that those actions were outside the legal scope of the monitors' duties and the training the monitors received, Bush said. The monitors' duties are to observe elections and document any perceived violations of federal voting laws, according to the nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center in Washington, D.C. The DOJ advised that the department would follow up with the monitors to prevent a recurrence, she said. Bush said there was also a media report out of Lansing that monitors were speaking to voters. But officials determined that those communications took place outside of the polling place after the voters had cast their ballots and that monitors advised the voters they were not required to speak with the monitors, making the communications with voters permissible, she said. A pair of Department of Justice observers, identified by a poll worker to the Lansing State Journal as Adam Candeub, and Justyne Tabler, watched voting at the Alfreda Schmidt Community Center in Lansing, spoke with Precinct 30 Chair Mary Morgan, and with some voters after they had cast their ballots. They asked at least some voters for their phone numbers in case they wished to contact them later. The Civil Rights Division of the DOJ has sent election monitors to cities in Michigan and across the nation for years. This year, the department said it was sending 1,000 monitors to all 50 states in what it described as the largest monitoring exercise ever. In Michigan, monitors were sent to Detroit, Dearborn, East Lansing, Flint, Grand Rapids, Hamtramck, Lansing and Warren. Angela Benander, chief communications officer for the Michigan Department of State, said the tabulator problems around the state were not anything out of the ordinary for a general election with strong turnout. Poll workers are trained to give voters the option of waiting until the tabulator problem is resolved, if they want to put their ballots into the tabulators themselves, or to place their ballots in an auxiliary bin to be fed into the tabulator later, she said. "It is ... pretty common to have blips and tech issues with election equipment on Election Day," Benander said during a 1 p.m. online briefing with reporters on Nov. 3. Benander said she'd heard no reports of voters being turned away from polling places because of tabulator problems: "We have not had any reports today of anything widespread, unusual, or anything that would cause us general concern." Department of State officials confirmed there were tabulator problems at Thurston High School in Redford Township and at Eisenhower High School in Shelby Township. A voter in Madison Heights also reported a problem with a broken tabulator at Wilkinson Middle School, which was confirmed by the Michigan ACLU. Lindsay White, a Madison Heights small business owner and community organizer who encountered a malfunctioning tabulator at her polling place, said in a Nov. 3 interview with the Detroit Free Press she wanted to wait with her ballot to ensure her vote was counted but ultimately opted to place the ballot in the auxiliary bin after the delay became protracted. White said she reported the incident to 1-866-Our-Vote, a nonpartisan hotline operated by the Michigan ACLU and other groups. Ann Mullen, a spokesperson for the Michigan ACLU, said problems with tabulators around the state are common in every election, but "poll workers have gotten far better through training on using the secure auxiliary bin for ballots, which are later tabulated with both a Republican and Democrat poll worker present." — The Lansing State Journal contributed to this report.

articles.title: National and state labor leaders rally in Detroit for Democratic candidates
articles.description: DETROIT — National AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler joined state labor leaders at a Detroit union hall Tuesday morning to rally for Democrats in the final stretch of a midterm election that has drawn national and international scrutiny. Schuler spoke alongside Democratic Attorney General nominee Eli Savit, renowned civil rights activist Charles Mauldin and others at […]
articles.content: AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler addresses supporters at the UNITE HERE Local 24’s Detroit office on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Minnah Arshad/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — National AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler joined state labor leaders at a Detroit union hall Tuesday morning to rally for Democrats in the final stretch of a midterm election that has drawn national and international scrutiny. Schuler spoke alongside Democratic Attorney General nominee Eli Savit, renowned civil rights activist Charles Mauldin and others at a canvass launch at UNITE HERE Local 24’s office, a hospitality workers’ union that is a part of AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the nation. “I don’t know about y’all, but I’m sick of the TV ads. Every state I’ve been to, it’s nothing but division. It’s nothing but toxicity and attacks, and you know why they’re doing that,” Shuler said to a packed room of mostly Black supporters donning Unite Here! shirts. “They know if the working class comes together and unites around these issues, that they’re toast.” Schuler said the labor community has a unique ability to cut through the noise of the political ads that have inundated Michigan’s airwaves. “We open people’s ears in a way that no one else does,” she said. Democratic attorney general nominee Eli Savit addresses supporters at the UNITE HERE Local 24’s Detroit office on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Minnah Arshad/Michigan Advance) Shuler’s presence in Detroit reflects the high stakes of the election, and of turnout in the Black-majority city. In the U.S. Senate election, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Republican nominee Mike Rogers have battled to win over the city’s residents. Black voters, a strong Democratic voting bloc, make up about 14% of the state’s population, and the party will likely need strong turnout among people of color to win. Antonio George, the Michigan political director of Unite Here Local 24, told Michigan Advance that the surprise endorsement by Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens’ of Rogers on Sunday was a “real big hit in the gut, especially for working people, especially for this union specifically.” Unite Here Local 24 had endorsed Stevens in the primary, then rallied behind El-Sayed in the general election. “For [Stevens] to cross lines like that, you tell the unions, you’re telling the Detroit residents, we don’t matter,” George said. He said union members were angry and surprised by her announcement on Sunday, and her appearance with the Trump-endorsed candidate at a predominantly Black church in Detroit was especially offensive. Civil rights leader Charles Mauldin addresses supporters at the UNITE HERE Local 24’s Detroit office on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Minnah Arshad/Michigan Advance) For the general election, George said Unite Here has knocked 150,000 doors for El-Sayed and he plans to continue canvassing before the polls close Tuesday. Mauldin, who was a student leader in the Selma, Alabama, civil rights protests in the 1960s, began his address at the canvas launch by leading a rendition of Woke Up this Morning With My Mind Stayed on Jesus. In a “Black Voters for Abdul” t-shirt, Mauldin said he’s spent the last 10 days traveling across the state to rally for Democrats. “I don’t have an office to run for but I’m here to run for you. I’m a foot soldier,” he said. “A foot soldier is a person who does a lot of work, but doesn’t need a lot of credit.” AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler and Democratic attorney General nominee Eli Savit talk with supporters at the UNITE HERE Local 24’s Detroit office on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Minnah Arshad/Michigan Advance) Savit said in one of his final addresses since launching his campaign in May 2025 that the last few months have been marked by a “divisive, cynical attempt funded by Elon Musk and his allies” to pit communities against one another and to prove that people of different races, religions and backgrounds can’t stand together. “Well we’re gonna send them a goddamn message tonight,” Savit said. Savit told the Advance after the event that he’s optimistic and excited about the Democratic Party’s chances Tuesday night. “Labor and working people built the state, so there’s no better way to end our campaign to spend Election Day than with our friends in labor.”

articles.title: Warren educator honored by the Michigan Lottery
articles.content: A Macomb County educator who was inspired by the importance of education instilled by his mother has been honored with an Excellence in Education award from the Michigan Lottery. The award winner, Brian Michael, is an English teacher for Fitzgerald High School, which is part of the Fitzgerald Public School District in Warren. The Michigan Lottery established the Excellence in Education awards in 2014 to recognize outstanding public-school educators across the state during the school year. Winners of the weekly award receive a $2,000 cash prize. At the end of the school year, one of the weekly award winners will be selected to receive the Lottery’s Educator of the Year award and will receive a $10,000 cash prize. Michael said his mother was a preschool teacher for more than 35 years. Seeing the passion and love she put into her work inspired him to become a teacher, he said. “As I grew up, I was fortunate to have had extraordinary teachers who helped shape me as a person and showed me the impact that a teacher can have on a student’s life,” he said in a news release. “I think I always knew that wherever life took me, that I wanted to make an impact somehow and in some way; to see what my own teachers did for me growing up and seeing the heart and dedication that my mom would put into her job teaching preschool, I thought ‘Why not give back and try to do the same for the next generation?’ With that, going into teaching felt like the natural career choice and I’ve never regretted it since.” Michael was nominated for the award by a former student, who called him an “extraordinary figure” at Fitzgerald High School. The anonymous nominator referred to him as a “parent, mentor, friend, and a constant source of inspiration to all students. ” Michael earned both a bachelor’s degree and a master’s degree from Oakland University and has been a teacher for 13 years, the last 10 in his current position.

articles.content: Google is completely turning off Search in schools that reject its AI features, the company told The New York Times. The decision was also shared in a broader education-related update from Google on Tuesday, saying that access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search “will be entirely off” for K-12 student accounts unless “administrators explicitly turn them on.” Administrators will not be given the option to toggle Gemini-powered features off without disabling Search, however. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the NYT, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” adding that schools that disable Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.” Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment. The announcement comes just months after Google turned its Gemini AI assistant on by default inside the Google Classroom app, which is used by more than 150 million teachers and students globally. The move added to skepticism surrounding Google’s introduction of AI in schools amid reports of declining test scores and other impacts on students’ learning abilities. Last month, lawmakers pressed Google on the “potential harms” of putting its AI products in schools. Although Google is no longer turning on AI features in schools by default, this choice comes at a cost. Several lawmakers and local leaders have responded to Google’s move to block Search, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (D-VT) calling it “extortion” and NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani saying, “no corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.” Rohit Chopra, California’s Secretary of Business & Consumer Services, wrote that Big Tech shouldn’t be able to “strong-arm schools.” Google argues that this change will “give schools more choice, not less,” adding that schools can choose to turn off each service on or off individually. The company is also attempting to address concerns about students using its AI features to find “shortcuts” instead of solving problems themselves. Google is embedding its Guided Learning feature, which is supposed to help students work through problems, into its AI Overviews in Search. Google will begin testing this feature in select US schools this month. Update, November 3rd: Added responses from lawmakers and Google.

articles.content: Early action can save lives, protect children and reduce future humanitarian costs, says UNICEF. As Malawi and neighbouring countries gear up to face the strongest El Niño on record, UNICEF is calling for urgent, flexible funding so that supplies, services and partners are in place before drought, flooding and disease reach children. Forecasters expect erratic rains, long dry spells and local flooding between October 2026 and March 2027. Already, 2.6 million people in Malawi face crisis levels of hunger, and cholera could return. Children and women will be hit hardest. UNICEF Representative in Malawi, Dr. Penelope Campbell said. “We can see this climate crisis coming, so we have a choice. If we act now, we can screen and treat children for malnutrition, keep water safe and keep children learning, before roads are cut off and before needs peak. Waiting would cost more in money, and in children's lives and futures," El Niño threatens to make three existing dangers worse: hunger, floods and cholera. El Niño's full effects take around 18 months to unfold. Under a severe drought scenario, up to 6 million more people could need humanitarian help by the 2028 lean season, the months before harvest when food runs short. A plan to reach nearly one million people UNICEF is supporting the Government's 2026/27 National El Niño Preparedness Plan, led by the Department of Disaster Management Affairs. Through this plan, UNICEF aims to reach 958,172 people directly in nine high-risk districts: Balaka, Blantyre, Chikwawa, Machinga, Mulanje, Mwanza, Nkhotakota, Nsanje and Phalombe. The plan includes: Some supplies are already stored in warehouses in Lilongwe, Blantyre and Bangula. Partners and rapid response teams are ready in every priority district. Further supplies are expected to arrive later this week. UNICEF Malawi needs US$7.61 million for its preparedness and response plan from August 2026 to March 2027. It has US$2.07 million so far, leaving a gap of US$5.54 million, or 73 per cent of the plan. “Acting early is better value,” added Dr. Penelope Campbell. “Every US$1 spent on reducing disaster risk saves up to US$15 in recovery costs. Every US$1 invested in nutrition returns about US$23. Flexible support now lets us prevent harm, not just respond to it." articles.title: Detentions, resignations, probes shake Serbia after students toppled strongman Vucic in election
articles.description: Detentions, resignations, probes shake Serbia after students toppled strongman Vucic in election AP News Serbia’s Graduation Day | Tim Judah The New York Review of Books How Serbia’s Students Unseated Aleksandar Vučić The National Interest Belgrade Diary: Election Day in Serbia, by Lily Lynch The Paris Review Serbia’s Gen Z Students Toppled a Strongman. Now Comes the Hard Part. WSJ
articles.content: BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Detentions, resignations, switching of sides, attempts to destroy evidence of wrongdoing. News has been coming in at such a pace in the wake of former Serbian strongman Aleksandar Vucic’s electoral defeat on Oct. 25 that a website dubbed “system breakdown” has been set up anonymously, with AI feeding information in real time. From high school students accusing their principal of throwing away documentation to the closure of a bank linked by local media to Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party, the public has been gripped by the fast-moving developments in the postelection week. Somewhat chaotic reports are seen by many in Serbia as a sign that Vucic’s carefully crafted power system is collapsing swiftly following the stunning victory of a student movement at the early parliamentary ballot. The Students’ List winners are yet to formally take over power in the government administration, security agencies and the army. But the seismic shift in the balance of power is pushing events to unfold before the actual takeover takes place. Despite the electoral defeat, a defiant Vucic — now described as the leader of the opposition — has continued with his daily appearances on loyal media, accusing the student-led movement of “revolutionary terror” and vowing to fight back. On Sunday evening, Vucic told Pink TV that “naturally, this is hard for my family and those who love me, but I am ready for everything and I will persist through anything.” Denying crime links, Vucic said he is not afraid of possible arrest because there will be no evidence against him. “I don’t sign anything … and nothing will be found,” he said. “They don’t have anything.” Officials jailed so far include Vucic’s chief of criminal police, Marko Kricak, and another senior police official, both suspected of abuse of office in connection with a high-profile murder investigation. Kricak was notorious over accusations that he personally threatened a female student with rape during anti-government protests, but he was not jailed over those allegations. On Monday, authorities also detained Davor Macura, the owner of private Alta Bank, whose license has been revoked. Macura is suspected of trying to take millions of dollars out of the bank’s vault and faces charges of abuse of office, according to prosecutors. While waiting to form the new government, the election winners have called on prosecutors and judges to start doing their jobs or step down. Scores of investigations into alleged top-level corruption cases remained incomplete under the previous government, including one into a Nov. 1, 2024, train station tragedy that triggered two years of student-led anti-graft protests. Now, the Serbian public is waiting to hear what will come out of a review into some of the longstanding probes after the student movement promised there will no longer be untouchable officials. In a statement on Tuesday, the Higher Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade complained of “an atmosphere of persecution and lynching,” after the election, along with “open political pressure by some social and political actors.” The statement said the alleged pressure was designed to force resignations and that the European Union mission in Belgrade and the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe have been informed. Prosecutors have been swamped with new complaints over incidents that vary from suspected election fraud to threats and violence against protesters, journalists and activists. Organized crime prosecutors also initiated procedures to determine whether some of them had been placed under illegal surveillance. On Monday, lawyer Ivan Ninic alleged a “criminal conspiracy” involving a justice ministry official and over three dozen prison wardens across Serbia, saying they pressured or bribed inmates to vote for Vucic during last week’s ballot. Ninic presented what he said were screenshots of online chats, with officials exchanging information about how many votes they managed to gather — Vucic’s SNS won overwhelmingly in Serbia’s prisons. In Mali Zvornik, on the border with Bosnia, police detained six people accused of granting false residence papers to Bosnian citizens so they could vote for Vucic’s party at the election. Some of the mainstream media in Serbia that were at the forefront of Vucic’s propaganda machinery have been the first to regroup. Previously staunchly pro-Vucic media outlets quickly adopted a more neutral position, while some television channels canceled chunks of their programs altogether and owners reportedly fled the country. State RTS television overhauled its leadership and apologized to its viewers for unprofessional reporting. But some of Vucic’s main mouthpieces, like broadcasters Informer and Pink, remain loyal, hosting the former leader daily in their programs. The election was for Serbia’s 250-member parliament and did not include local governments across the country. Now, calls are mounting for early municipal elections. Vucic’s SNS lost in the capital, Belgrade, and most other towns, after it previously controlled the country down to every village, with the exception of one urban municipality in the southern city of Nis. Throughout Serbia, employees in theaters, museums, culture associations, schools and hospitals are demanding that SNS-appointed managers immediately step down. In Belgrade, Fifth High School principal Ognjen Mrvaljevic denied that he was throwing away relevant school documentation, N1 television reported. He said in comments carried by local media that he was just getting rid of unnecessary papers. Vucic’s party’s “expiration date has passed,” analyst Slobodan Stupar said. “It will all fall like dominoes.”

What is call transcription? A practical business guide
articles.description: Learn what call transcription is, how it works, and how to transcribe phone calls with AI. Compare software types and see a sample transcript.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Call transcription is the process of turning a phone or video call into written text. These calls are often full of valuable information, with an accurate written transcript making it easy to find data for reference. In business settings such as customer support, call transcription is also helpful for training and compliance. Instead of hand-transcribing every phone call, many teams now use AI-powered speech to text transcription to automate the process. In this article, we’ll break down how call transcription works, why it’s important, and how to transcribe your calls automatically using AI. Call transcription involves converting a phone call or video call into a written text format. The call transcription provides a record of exactly what was said and when. With a written transcript, you can review the call later without having to listen to the entire audio file. This process is usually done with automated call transcription software, although it can also be done manually. With automated transcription software, the process happens in real time during the call or shortly after the call ends. Call transcription is a multi-step process. Across these steps, you’ll end up with a final transcript that is searchable and serves as a digital record of a conversation. Especially if companies want a living corpus of records that they can feed into AI tools to get recommendations or insights at scale, having these call transcripts is invaluable. In a business setting, the steps above usually sit inside a larger pipeline: If you build voice AI agents with ElevenAgents, call transcripts are saved with each conversation. You’ll be able to review them at scale without having to build out the entire pipeline yourself. Here’s a quick call transcript example to demonstrate what post-recording transcription will produce. A formatted call transcript shows who spoke and when: [00:00:02] Agent: Thanks for calling Acme Support. How can I help? [00:00:05] Caller: Hi, I’d like to check the status of my order. [00:00:09] Agent: Of course. Can I have your order number? Timestamps and speaker labels make it easy to search a transcript and jump to the right moment in the audio. Call transcription creates a record of the phone and video calls that happen within an organization, which prevents important information from getting lost. Here are a few of the ways that businesses use phone transcription in their operations. Many organizations put their call transcripts into an internal database. Team members can search for specific pieces of information from previous calls, rather than having to review entire transcripts manually. Sales and customer service teams often use call transcripts to improve their performance. Managers will review transcripts to make sure associates are meeting expectations and find opportunities for improvement. Organizations that are subject to strict compliance standards, such as HIPAA, GDPR, or SEC regulations, often use call transcripts to prove they are meeting these requirements when interacting with clients and business partners. These transcripts help protect the organization in the event of an audit. Many organizations integrate call transcription tools with their CRM. After a call with a client, the transcript goes directly to that client’s digital profile. These transcripts eliminate the need for manual note-taking during calls. It also ensures that all team members have access to the same client information, even if they weren’t on the original call. This helps organizations provide a more personalized, responsive customer experience. Recording captures the audio from a phone or video call, while transcription converts that audio file into a text file. Real-time transcription models can also convert an audio live stream into text without a pre-recorded file. Call recording and call transcription are two separate processes, although many teams use them together. Both create a record of what happened on a call so you can revisit the information later. However, you can also use these two processes individually. If you just need an audio file, you can record a call without transcribing it. You can also transcribe existing audio files in your library, even if they were recorded a long time ago. To transcribe a phone or video call with automatic transcription, send the audio from the call to a speech to text API, such as ElevenLabs Scribe v2. The API will convert the audio into a formatted transcript with timestamps and speaker labels. Once the transcript is ready, you can download and export it in your preferred file format. ElevenLabs supports a variety of options, including plain text, HTML, PDF, DOCX, JSON, SRT, and VTT. You can also use the speech to text API to send your transcripts directly to other programs in your tech stack. You have two options for automatic call transcription: transcribing an audio recording after it’s finished, or transcribing an audio live stream as it’s happening. The right choice for your team will depend on your priorities and how you’re using your call recordings. Transcribing finished audio recordings is the more cost-effective option, so it works well if your team needs to transcribe dozens of calls each week. It’s also more accurate, making it a better choice for high-stakes meetings or compliance documentation. If speed is a top priority, use a real-time model with server-side streaming instead. Real-time models provide instant meeting notes you can reference right after the call. Real-time transcription also makes calls more accessible and easier to follow. If a participant is a non-native speaker or is hard of hearing, they can reference the transcript as the call is happening for support. While building a call transcription pipeline with a STT API is great for working at scale, you don’t necessarily need a developer to transcribe a call. Record the call with your phone system or a call recording app, upload the audio file to a speech to text tool such as ElevenCreative Speech to Text, and download the transcript. Here’s what to consider when choosing a call transcription software for your business. Many transcription models accurately transcribe audio captured in a studio with a professional microphone, but struggle to process audio captured on a phone or video call. When transcribing calls, you need an AI model with consistently high accuracy rates, even when audio quality isn’t perfect. You’ll also need a model that accurately processes a wide range of accents and dialects. With the current integrated global economy, your team will likely be meeting with clients and colleagues from around the world, and you need clear, accurate transcripts for every meeting. If your company operates internationally, you will need a platform that supports multiple languages. Accurate speaker labeling is essential when transcribing calls. When choosing an AI transcription tool, opt for a platform that consistently and accurately separates speakers, even when their voices sound similar. Behind the scenes, this is called speaker diarization: the process of detecting who is speaking and when, and labeling each speaker in the transcript. On phone calls, diarization is what lets you tell the agent from the customer. Learn more in our guide to speaker diarization. The transcript should also contain accurate timestamps for each speaker. Timestamps make it easy to find specific moments in the transcript later. In jurisdictions with a one-party consent law, any active participant in a conversation can record and transcribe it, without obtaining explicit consent from the other participants. In jurisdictions with an all-party consent law, everyone on the call must be notified and give permission before the recording starts. If a call is taking place across multiple jurisdictions, callers should adhere to the stricter all-party consent law. The easiest way to do this is notify all participants of the recording and transcription at the beginning of the call. Continued participation in the call is generally treated as implied consent. Retaining call transcripts is generally legal as long as the recording itself was legal. However, some privacy laws, such as GDPR or CCPA, may limit how long you can keep recordings if they contain sensitive consumer data. Some regulations may also require you to anonymize recordings that contain this information. articles.content: Early voting at Kearny Town Hall in Kearny, New Jersey, on Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)WASHINGTON — Tens of millions of Americans have already cast a ballot in the 2026 midterm elections that will determine control of Congress and shape President Donald Trump’s remaining policy agenda. As of Monday, more than 57 million Americans had cast a vote, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, which tracks early voting. This year’s elections have already shattered the record for midterm early voting, set in 2022, in which nearly 46 million Americans voted early. Polls close between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m. local time on Election Day. Under federal law, as long as voters are in line when the polls close, they can still cast their ballots. Voters must be at least 18 years old, a U.S. citizen and registered to vote in their state. Many states allow same-day registration. Trump came into his second term with his party in control of both chambers of Congress. But historically, the president’s party loses seats in the midterm elections, and this cycle appears unlikely to be an exception. Elections forecasters have favored Democrats to win back the majority in the U.S. House, which would allow them to significantly rein in Trump’s legislative agenda. Analysts have also increasingly predicted Democrats could win control of the U.S. Senate could, which would allow them to block appointments, including a potential U.S. Supreme Court vacancy. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter projects Democrats to pick up a Senate seat in North Carolina and lists six more races as toss-ups, all of which are now held by Republicans. Those races are in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas. Democrats are defending an open seat in Michigan that the Cook Political Report moved from toss-up to leaning toward the Democrat, Abdul El-Sayed, on Monday. If the other races go as predicted, Democrats would have to win at least three of the toss-ups to gain control of the chamber. The Cook Political Report shifted 12 House races in the direction of Democrats on Oct. 30. Eighteen remained toss-ups as of Monday. Democrats have to net three seats to flip control of the House, if they also win the race in a heavily Democratic Florida district that is vacant after former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick resigned in April. If Democrats gain the majority in the House, they are likely to pursue investigations into Trump and other administration officials. They have also signaled they will embrace a policy agenda centered on lowering costs, especially related to healthcare, though Trump’s veto looms on any major legislation Congress passes for the next two years. Legal challenges amid dismal numbers The war with Iran that has contributed to high gas and diesel prices, inflation and an aggressive immigration crackdown has led to historically low presidential approval ratings. Trump’s approval on average was at 37% Monday, only a tick better than his second-term low of 36% recorded just two weeks earlier, according to The New York Times. The president has already made an attempt to use the Department of Justice to halt the certification of the Alaska U.S. Senate race, after The New York Times reported the campaign of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola made an effort to recruit a candidate with the same name as GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan in order to stack the four-way general election in her favor. States Newsroom has not independently verified the Times story. A federal judge tossed out the lawsuit Sunday. Other court challenges related to the administration’s actions or potential actions related to the election are still unfolding on Election Day. Cases include Democrats’ aim to bar armed federal officials for polling locations and DOJ’s effort to prevent California from counting 20,000 votes the Trump administration suspects are noncitizens. The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday denied the Trump administration’s final attempt to force California to set aside the ballots. Separately, congressional Democrats have taken their own precautions. More than 100 Senate staffers and 300 House staffers were trained as election monitors and will be sent to 60 or 70 close races, the top Democrat on the House Administration Committee, Joe Morelle, told reporters last week. Even after the polls close, it could take weeks to know the results of some races, and consequently, control of both chambers of Congress, due to each state’s voting laws and processes for counting votes. After the 2022 midterms, control of the House was projected for Republicans eight days after Election Day. In 2024, the same projection took nine days.

articles.title: Commentary: Permitting reform bill will decimate protections in the National Historic Preservation Act
articles.description: On September 30, 2026, a permitting reform bill was introduced in the U.S. Senate that would significantly weaken the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). The NHPA was passed in 1966 after thousands of historic places around the U.S. were demolished during urban renewal efforts in 1950s and 1960s. The loss of buildings like Penn Station […]
articles.content: Because archaeological resources in Michigan are often buried, Sec. 106 reviews require identification through methods such as shovel testing or excavation. This photo, courtesy of the Michigan State Historic Preservation Office, is of work being conducted in the Detroit neighborhood known as Paradise Valley.On September 30, 2026, a permitting reform bill was introduced in the U.S. Senate that would significantly weaken the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). The NHPA was passed in 1966 after thousands of historic places around the U.S. were demolished during urban renewal efforts in 1950s and 1960s. The loss of buildings like Penn Station in New York City produced fierce public outcry because the demolition had occurred without any public review process. In Michigan, it was the destruction of Old City Hall in Detroit 1961 and the demolition of whole neighborhoods for new highways that prompted Michigan’s own reckoning. Because of these demolitions when the NHPA was passed it included a provision known as Section 106 which required that any federally funded, licensed, or permitted project be evaluated to determine if historic properties would be negatively affected and it requires that state and local governments, Tribal Nations, and the public be provided the opportunity to comment on these projects. Public input is a specific remedy baked into the NHPA after we learned hard lessons in the rubble of our discontent, the realization dawning that we had no means to preserve our significant places while we sorted through the actual rubble of Penn Station, Old City Hall, and thousands of other places. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act obliterates the public notice and input requirements that were purposefully inserted into the NHPA. Imagine a data center project that requires a federal permit because it’s close to a wetland: if passed, this bill will remove the requirement that federal agencies solicit the public’s input, rather, the public will only learn about federally permitted destruction when the bulldozers arrive on site. The bill contains additional, highly concerning provisions including narrowing the project types that trigger the Section 106 process in the first place. For instance, it excludes projects that utilize federal loans, grants, and other financial assistance which means that Federal Highway Administration projects, (which are typically funded by grants distributed to states) will largely be excluded from the Section 106 process. Perhaps some of the most egregious changes in this bill pertain to Tribal Nations. Today, Tribal Nations are key constituents in the Section 106 process because they steward their sacred places and ancestral lands. To ensure these places are accounted for, the Section 106 process requires archeological survey for areas where ground disturbance is proposed. For example, in 2026, an FCC-permitted cell phone tower project in Charlevoix County required ground disturbance and, during the survey work, a Native American burial place was discovered. After discussing this discovery with the State Historic Preservation Office and the Little Traverse Bay Band of Odawa Indians, it was decided that the best path forward was to redesign the project to avoid the burial site completely. This early identification exemplifies the importance of the Section 106 process under the current law which requires consultation with interested parties like Tribal Nations. In new collaborations, tribes become stewards of parks and monuments But the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will gut this process as it relates to Tribes because it will make consultation with Tribal Nations optional and it would allow federal agencies to unilaterally decide which Tribal sites are sacred enough to protect. Moreover, the bill has provisions that violate tribal sovereignty because it will allow the federal government to take over tribal preservation offices if they function in a way that displeases the federal government. This bill was hastily written. Key terms are not defined and, when asked what certain terms mean, the drafters admitted they couldn’t agree on definitions, leaving courts to sort it out. This bill will not streamline projects; it will cause confusion and prompt excessive litigation. Most people likely don’t realize that architects, archaeologists, architectural historians, and Tribal Nation leaders work every day to protect historic places via the Section 106 process, quietly enfranchising diverse voices in the process. At a time when some of our most important historic places are under threat, it is vital that we speak up when bad legislation is proposed and this bill is about as bad as it gets for historic places, places we cannot put back together once the wrecking ball starts swinging.

The ElevenLabs IPO prep discussion gives investors a timeline to follow, but it does not establish a listing date. His comments arrive as the voice startup expands into enterprise communications, where winning a contract and building a predictable business are different achievements. Speaking with Bloomberg’s Tom Mackenzie in London on November 3, Staniszewski said he would like to take ElevenLabs public. He also described an initial public offering, the first public sale of a company’s shares, as one step in a longer journey. The emphasis was on readiness rather than a guaranteed transaction. That distinction frames the story. ElevenLabs wants enterprise voice agents to become lasting business infrastructure, while prospective public investors will need evidence that customers keep using them profitably. Amazon’s competing voice technology provides another reference point: demand for spoken AI does not automatically establish which supplier captures the value. The CEO outlined a readiness ambition, leaving the timing and terms of any eventual offering open. Bloomberg’s published IPO interview captures a narrower statement than a scheduled stock market debut. Asked whether 2028 was a reasonable timeframe, Staniszewski emphasized preparing the company and establishing the necessary foundations. He did not announce an exchange, offering structure, or transaction date in that answer. The wording matters because preparation and execution describe different decisions. A company can improve its reporting, management processes, and financial planning while retaining flexibility over when to seek public investors. Those steps can also support a larger private business. This is the useful way to read the ElevenLabs IPO timeline explained by its chief executive. The year provides a planning horizon. It does not tell readers when shares will become available or whether market conditions will support an offering then. Nor does the comment establish that meaningful preparation must wait until 2028. Staniszewski discussed running the business with public-company expectations over the coming years. Treating the year as an absolute starting line would lose that part of his answer. An important consequence follows for how subsequent news should be interpreted. A finance appointment, governance change, or reporting update would be consistent with readiness work. None would independently prove that a listing had been approved or scheduled. Conversely, the absence of an immediate transaction announcement would not contradict the stated goal. Readiness is an organizational condition; a public offering is an event requiring additional decisions. Collapsing those concepts creates expectations the interview does not support. For employees, customers, and developers, the announcement therefore carries a different meaning than it does for people seeking an investment opportunity. It signals how management wants the company to mature. It provides little immediate information about ownership access or transaction mechanics. The business implications deserve more attention than calendar speculation. Those are observable features of the company before any eventual offering. There is also a limit to what can be inferred from executive intent. The rest of the analysis concerns whether enterprise communications can supply the durable business that ambition requires. In its enterprise adoption update, the company said enterprise customers accounted for 55% of revenue. Still, it explains why an IPO discussion now centers on business communications. Management is presenting enterprise interaction as a substantial part of the company’s commercial identity. The pressure falls first on ElevenLabs’ deployment and support teams. A generated narration can be evaluated as an output. An agent, software that responds to requests and performs permitted actions, must function inside an ongoing business process. Consider an illustrative customer-service interaction involving an account question. A pleasant voice helps establish the conversation, but the system also needs accurate information and appropriate permissions. It must recognize when the request exceeds its authority. If that interaction fails, responsibility does not end with the speech model. The customer experiences the full service, including delays, incorrect answers, repeated questions, and transfers. An enterprise buyer therefore evaluates a wider set of responsibilities than a voice demonstration reveals. That changes the demands on sales as well. A convincing demonstration can earn a trial, but a business buyer needs a reason to expand deployment. Evidence of resolved requests matters more than an impressive opening exchange. Customer operations teams face a related decision. They must decide which requests software should handle and which require a person. Automating an unsuitable interaction can shift work elsewhere rather than remove it. For developers, the consequence is a broader integration burden. The voice interface must connect to business knowledge, account systems, and approved actions. Each connection introduces dependencies that affect the final customer experience. These are analytical implications of the enterprise strategy, not disclosed performance results for ElevenLabs. The available announcements establish management’s direction. They do not quantify every operational benefit or implementation expense. The distinction becomes especially important when evaluating ElevenLabs enterprise voice agents. Adoption can show that organizations want the product. It does not establish that every deployment follows the same economics or requires the same support. Over time, the relevant question becomes whether delivery grows more repeatable. A business that can reuse deployment methods has different operating characteristics from one requiring extensive custom work for each account. That is why the readiness ambition creates pressure now, despite its distant horizon. Enterprise customers need dependable service today, while management must build processes capable of supporting future scale. It also describes engineers working directly with the telecom company during integration. The account includes the Magenta AI Call Assistant, unveiled at Mobile World Congress in March 2026. Proposed functions included contextual assistance, translation during calls, and summaries available afterward. These are distinct tasks with different requirements. A translation feature must preserve meaning across languages. A summary must capture the relevant information without introducing unsupported details. An assistant performing a task must understand what it is authorized to do. The same spoken interface can therefore hide very different operational challenges. This is an analytical observation about the product category, rather than evidence that the partnership has failed. It explains why deployment detail matters when assessing the business. The partnership also offers a supportive customer perspective. In ElevenLabs’ account, Deutsche Telekom executives emphasize trust, reliability, and close collaboration. Their comments suggest that voice quality helps customers engage, while implementation requires work across the wider system. That perspective is valuable, but its publication context matters. The material appears in a supplier-produced customer story. It supports the existence and scope of the collaboration without independently establishing its financial return. For prospective investors, the engineering involvement introduces a practical question. Does hands-on implementation create reusable knowledge that makes subsequent deployments easier? Or does each large customer continue to require substantial dedicated effort? The answer affects how enterprise growth should be interpreted. Both approaches can generate useful products and satisfied customers. They can nevertheless produce different staffing needs, delivery schedules, and opportunities for operating efficiency. A closer connection to customer systems can also strengthen the supplier relationship. Replacing a voice component is different from replacing a service embedded in business workflows. The latter decision involves more organizational work. However, integration should not be treated as proof that customers cannot switch.
