articles.description: While much of the national attention on today’s midterm elections has focused on control of Congress, voters across the country will also choose which party controls the levers of state power. Across the states, more than 6,000 legislative seats are up for grabs, leaving the partisan control of numerous chambers hanging in the balance. And […]
articles.content: Republican Rick Jackson rallies supporters in Roswell, Georgia, last week as he campaigned for Georgia governor. This year, voters in 36 states will elect governors with at least a dozen races characterized by analysts as competitive. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)While much of the national attention on today’s midterm elections has focused on control of Congress, voters across the country will also choose which party controls the levers of state power. Across the states, more than 6,000 legislative seats are up for grabs, leaving the partisan control of numerous chambers hanging in the balance. And voters will choose governors in 36 states. Only a dozen of those races are considered competitive by independent analysts, but Democrats have a shot at winning control of a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years. Midterm elections generally favor the party that doesn’t control the White House. Voters’ growing disapproval of President Donald Trump and frustration over high prices has given Democrats a shot at not only flipping control of Congress but also making major gains in state governments, where Republicans have held a majority of governors and legislative chambers since 2010. “For the most part the Republicans are kind of playing defense more than offense,” Katy Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting at the National Conference of State Legislatures, told Stateline earlier this election cycle. Currently, Republicans boast a 26-24 gubernatorial advantage over Democrats. The math could change depending on the outcome of today’s elections, particularly as Democrats are competing closely in some reliably conservative states. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, which ranks the competitiveness of state and national races, identified a dozen races for governor considered competitive this cycle. Those include: Alaska, Georgia, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska, Nevada, Ohio, Oregon, Texas and Wisconsin. In recent weeks, Cook moved its ratings of the Florida and Texas governor races from Likely Republican to Lean Republican. That means the GOP candidates are still favored in those states, but “given the grim political environment for the GOP,” the analysts could not rule out an upset in one or both states. Democrats’ improving prospects are evidence of the broader political challenges facing Republicans across the country, said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston. “It’s a rebuke of the Trump model, and especially the Republican Trump model,” he said. “But it’s also something that isn’t uncommon for midterms.” In states such as Alaska, Georgia, Florida, Iowa, Nebraska, Ohio and Texas, a Democratic governor could reinvigorate the left, which has struggled to compete with the GOP’s grip on state power, providing a new check on Republican lawmakers. Experts say Democratic control of more governor’s offices could mean more bipartisan compromise — or gridlock — in state capitols, depending on which party controls the legislature. In Nevada, a Democratic governor could initiate a new era of policymaking: Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo has vetoed more than 160 bills approved by the Democratic-controlled legislature during his term. Democrats are also aiming to flip hundreds of state legislative seats this cycle. Republicans currently boast control of 28 state legislatures and Democrats control 18, while three states have divided control of chambers, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Since President Donald Trump’s second term began, Democrats have flipped a dozen seats in special elections in Arkansas, Iowa, Florida, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Texas, according to tracking by the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, which works to elect Democrats at the state level. They also flipped another 18 seats in last year’s general elections in New Jersey and Virginia. Heather Williams, president of that organization, has repeatedly characterized 2026 as “a once-in-a-generation opportunity” to transform state legislative power for the party. The outcome of gubernatorial and legislative races will undoubtedly affect local policymaking in upcoming legislative sessions. But both parties have identified control of congressional redistricting as another prize up for grabs this cycle. Set off by a White House push to give Republicans more seats in the U.S. House, 10 states have completed middecade redistricting — a phenomenon unseen since the 1800s. “We know Democrats and their national allies will continue to pour millions into state legislative races because they understand what’s at stake: the legislators elected in 2026 will shape redistricting and the balance of power for years to come,” Republican State Leadership Committee President Edith Jorge-Tuñón, said in a July statement to Stateline. Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org. articles.content: Signs informed attendees at Lansing's No Kings protest on Oct. 17, 2026 of a nonpartisan voter protection and information hotline. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Election Day marks the culmination of months of campaigning in Michigan for races that will likely determine party control of crucial seats on both a state and federal level — including the U.S. Senate, governor’s office, a number of key U.S. House races and both chambers of the state Legislature. As of midafternoon Monday, the Michigan Department of State reported that more than 2.3 million Michiganders had already cast ballots, including more than 743,000 who voted in person at early voting sites and more than 1.5 million who returned absentee ballots by mail. For those who still have to cast their ballots, polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time in Michigan. While most of Michigan voters will be casting ballots in the Eastern Time Zone, four counties in the Upper Peninsula — Dickinson, Gogebic, Iron, and Menominee — use Central Time instead and won’t finish voting until 9 p.m. Eastern Time Concerns about a federal presence at the polls have been voiced throughout the election cycle, and local clerks throughout Michigan have worked to ease fears from potential voters. A test ballot is submitted to an early voting tabulator in the Lansing Elections Office prior to the August primary. July 20, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Advocates are also working to ensure voters know what to do if they do encounter election interference, law enforcement presence or any other problems while voting. The national, nonpartisan Election Protection Coalition has launched a hotline, 866-OUR-VOTE, for reporting voting problems and seeking assistance. Hotlines are also available in Spanish at 888-VE-Y-VOTA, in Arabic at 844-YALLA-US, and in Asian languages at 888-API-VOTE. Federal election monitors from the Department of Justice are expected in Detroit, East Lansing, Flint, Grand Rapids, Hamtramck, Lansing and Warren. Federal monitors are standard and have been present at elections around the country for years. They function as observers to ensure voters are able to freely cast their ballots, and in Michigan’s primary, were described by election officials as “polite and unobtrusive.” Andrew Walchuk, the policy director and counsel for Common Cause, did express concerns about a potential lack of proper training for DOJ poll watchers after the Civil Rights Division has been “decimated by this administration.” The real concern, however, comes if federal troops or armed federal law enforcement, including ICE, are present at polling places, which is illegal. A “Know Your Rights” flyer from the National Police Accountability Project explains that local police can be present if election officials or members of the public call for assistance — though “sustained law enforcement presence at a polling location could constitute voter intimidation or interference under state criminal law.” In Grand Rapids, advocates with GR Rapid Response to ICE are maintaining a hotline of their own, 616-238-0081, to report any local ICE presence. “If there are armed federal agents, whether they are from DHS or the FBI or any other federal entity, they’re not allowed to be there,” Walchuk said. “Federal law for 150 years has forbidden federal agents, armed agents, from being at the polls, and so that is something that, if anyone does see agents at the polls, they should call the hotline.” Michigan State University voting in 2020. (Photo by Anna Liz Nichols/Michigan Advance) Once polls close, results will not be immediately available, especially in elections that may come down to just a few percentage points. Though many concerns about election interference are centered on Election Day itself, advocates, including Jessica Ayoub, the deputy political director of the ACLU of Michigan, are also preparing to combat any interference in the election certification process. “Michigan law is clear: boards of county canvassers in Michigan must certify the election results based solely on the record of votes cast. They tally the votes and certify the results,” Ayoub said in a press call with the Election Protection Coalition. “The role of boards of county canvassers is not discretionary. Canvassers double check the math. They do not police our elections.” Ballotpedia’s summary of Michigan law states, “Automatic recounts are required if the vote differential between the two candidates is .1% or less for statewide elections, including ballot measures, 75 votes or less for state senate elections, and 25 votes or less for state house elections.” A candidate can also request a recount if they meet certain requirements and file a request officially “not later than 5 p.m. of the second day after the day the board of state canvassers certifies the results of the election.” In Michigan, canvassers are required to certify results no later than the 14th day after the election.

How Cisco defends at machine speed with OpenAI
articles.description: Cisco combines network intelligence with OpenAI models to strengthen enterprise security. Learn how it is building more adaptive defenses.
articles.content: Cisco combines network intelligence and OpenAI models to build more adaptive defenses. Cisco builds the networking and security infrastructure that organizations rely on to connect and protect their systems. As adversaries leverage AI to scale automated attacks and craft exploits at machine-speed, defending enterprise infrastructure must evolve. Pairing Cisco’s vast network telemetry with frontier AI reasoning gives defenders the toolkit necessary to outpace emerging threats. OpenAI’s rigorous approach to enterprise data privacy—centered on zero data retention, strict customer data boundaries, and verifiable isolation—means Cisco could confidently deploy frontier intelligence across mission-critical systems without compromising customer priorities or sensitive telemetry. Cisco’s defense starts where threats move: the network. Patel describes a shift from a single security perimeter to controls distributed across microservices, containers, and clusters. “We can put a mini security stack in front of every microservice, every Kubernetes container, and every Kubernetes cluster, and fuse security into the fabric of the network,” he says. Controls at the application level can restrict communication to the connections each service needs, reducing the paths an attacker can use to spread. Security teams can also isolate affected systems more selectively, allowing unaffected services to keep running while they investigate and respond. Combining that network intelligence with OpenAI’s models allows Cisco to correlate signals at machine scale, Patel says. “Two signals might seem benign in isolation, but together they can reveal a meaningful pattern. Network intelligence allows us to correlate data across the network and derive insights to inform secure operations.” Patel points to a pressing challenge for defenders: the gap between how quickly attackers can exploit a vulnerability and how long organizations take to patch it. He sees AI as a way to help narrow that gap, giving defenders the capacity to investigate more threats and respond faster. “AI hands attackers speed and scale. Using AI for defense is a prerequisite for staying safe,” he says. He describes initiatives like Daybreak and GPT‑6 Astra as advances that strengthen security for both Cisco and its customers. “We’re able to find and patch vulnerabilities more efficiently, while shortening the time needed for investigation, response, and remediation,” Patel says. Patel sees a path to adoption that builds on the processes teams already use to find and address vulnerabilities. “These capabilities can fit into your existing scanning workflows, so you don’t have to fundamentally change how your team works.” As agents become more autonomous, security teams also need to distinguish malicious interference from an agent pursuing a legitimate goal in an unintended way. Patel says that requires security telemetry alongside observability data, so teams can assess both threats and agent behavior. He outlines three priorities: protect agents from malicious attacks, detect and intercept unintended behavior, and operate in near real time. These priorities are guiding the shift towards policies and controls that can adapt as agents act. Through the Daybreak Defense Network, Cisco and OpenAI are exploring how to help security teams triage exposure faster and enforce the right controls in Cisco Cloud Control. For Patel, that can help shift the advantage back to defenders.

European troops prepare for a postwar Ukraine mission that’s fraught with challenges
articles.description: European troops prepare for a postwar Ukraine mission that’s fraught with challenges AP News UK and European peacekeepers in Ukraine would be allowed to fire back at Russians The Guardian Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace BBC In Poland, the 'Coalition of the Willing' holds first large-scale military exercise Le Monde.fr European force to hold first Ukraine support exercise
articles.content: LONDON (AP) — Thousands of European troops will take part in a military exercise in Poland this month to prepare for a hypothetical postwar mission in Ukraine to boost the country’s economy and rebuild its armed forces. But some experts say the deployment may never take place. The force’s first military exercise, led by Britain and France, is aimed both at testing deployment plans and sending a message to Russia and the Trump administration that European countries are stepping up militarily. Yet the overall mission is plagued with challenges, including the ongoing fighting, questions over American support and the outcome of the upcoming French elections. Britain and France are both part of a wider political group of 37 nations supporting Ukraine known as the Coalition of the Willing. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly said that in the event of a peace deal, there must be strong security guarantees from Kyiv’s Western allies, including the United States, to deter Russian President Vladimir Putin from attacking the country again. That’s where this force could come in. “This exercise shows the UK is stepping up, alongside France and our allies, to prepare for the day peace comes to Ukraine,” British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said. Alongside France and Britain, eight other European nations will deploy 2,800 soldiers to Poland to rehearse transporting people and equipment into Poland, conduct joint command and control drills and fly jets and an aerial refueling tanker in preparation to help Ukraine reopen its skies. If deployed once a ceasefire is in place, the force would help regenerate and strengthen Ukraine’s armed forces, provide the reassurance needed to open the country’s skies and help clear mines in the Black Sea, said Lt. Gen. Tom Bateman, commander of Multinational Force-Ukraine, or MNF-U. Here’s a look at the force and the serious challenges it faces. All of the European countries involved in the force say they will only deploy once hostilities cease. But for that to happen, there needs to be a ceasefire. Peace negotiations stalled earlier this year after U.S. President Donald Trump launched his war with Iran, while in September he said he had done a deal with Russia to supply diesel fuel to the U.S. ahead of the midterm elections in an attempt to lower fuel prices, providing a political and economic boost to the Kremlin. Trump also called for the removal of Zelenskyy and demanded Kyiv stop striking Russian energy infrastructure. Trump and his officials also offered confusing messages as to why Starshield — which Ukraine uses for drone strikes and air defense — had been throttled. In September, Zelenskyy said the U.S. had failed to provide warning, as it normally did, of incoming Russian ballistic missile attacks. While both Ukraine and Russia have signaled their willingness to resume U.S.-brokered peace talks, deep disagreements over territory and security guarantees remain. For Ukraine and European nations, a critical part of any agreement was a U.S. guarantee that it would support Kyiv with intelligence and help monitor a ceasefire, said Ed Arnold, a Senior Associate Fellow at the RUSI military think tank in London. But now, “the US are basically supporting Russia against Ukraine,” Arnold said, suggesting a lasting ceasefire could be a long way off. The troops will rehearse transporting people and equipment into Poland, conduct joint command and control drills and fly jets and an aerial refueling tanker in preparation to help Ukraine reopen its skies, the British and French defense ministries said. The initial idea of the Coalition of the Willing group of nations was to provide Ukraine with security guarantees similar to NATO’s Article 5, in which allies treat an attack against one member as an attack against the entire alliance and discuss how they would respond together, said Federico Santopinto, senior research fellow at the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs in Paris. NATO could have offered such security guarantees, but the U.S. and Germany refused that option, which is why France and the U.K. decided to go ahead with plans for a separate European proposal of countries willing to come to Ukraine’s aid if necessary, a French official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military details. But the European deployment will not be a NATO force, peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring mission and is “not designed for offensive operations.” Rather it is aimed at helping Ukraine deter future Russian aggression, said Bateman, the force commander. The exercise in Poland was planned earlier this year but is taking place at a time when several European nations, including Poland, have warned of the rising threat from Russian covert activity, including sabotage, espionage and drone incursions. Denmark’s Defense Intelligence Service said Putin may carry out military attacks against NATO only if he assesses NATO will not respond collectively and “especially if Russia assesses that the United States cannot or will not support the European NATO countries in a potential war against Russia.” Last year, Putin said that any foreign troops inside Ukraine would be considered “legitimate targets.” For that reason, any deployment needs to be a “combat force for their own force protection,” Arnold said, suggesting that if soldiers were pulled at the first sign of trouble, it would make Europe look weak. Santopinto also expressed skepticism about Europeans’ capacity to provide the “credible deterrence” against Russia that Ukraine would need. “That could mean having to shoot down Russian fighter jets, with the risk of escalation that everyone wants to avoid,” he said. “Would Europeans be prepared to directly intercept drones and missiles launched by Russia into Ukrainian airspace?” In France, meanwhile, next year’s presidential election is raising doubts about whether the proposed force could materialize. Centrist President Emmanuel Macron cannot seek a third consecutive term, and protests have added to the pressures facing his government. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, seen as the favorite, has opposed sending troops to Ukraine. Last month, she said she would end financial assistance to Kyiv after six months in office because France “can no longer afford it.” The party of far-left rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon also opposes a deployment. Other contenders on the left and right have warned against escalation, saying they are concerned about a wider European conflict. “This is a military operation in search of a mission,” facing many challenges, Arnold said. For that reason, he said, there is almost “zero” chance the force will ever deploy to Ukraine.
